questions.stem: A 25-year-old newly married woman wants effective contraception with a minimum failure rate. Which contraceptive method would be the most suitable for her considering both efficacy and ease of use?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old newly married woman wants effective contraception with a minimum failure rate. Which contraceptive method would be the most suitable for her considering both efficacy and ease of use?
questions.solution: Implants: The 3-year implant has one of the lowest failure rates at 0.05%, indicating high effectiveness. This method is suitable for a newly married woman who desires reliable contraception without daily adherence. The implant also offers long-term protection (up to 3 years) with minimal user intervention after insertion, making it convenient. Oral Pills (Option B): Effective with perfect use (0.3% failure), but higher failure with typical use (8%) due to daily dosing and missed pills. Implants are preferred for better compliance and efficacy. Condoms (Option C): Typical use failure rate is 15%, less reliable than implants. Offer dual protection (pregnancy & STIs), but not ideal for sole contraceptive use. IUD (Option D): Low failure rates—levonorgestrel IUD (0.2%) and copper T (0.8%)—but can cause menstrual irregularities, dysmenorrhea, and pelvic pain. Implants are often favored. Pearl Index: Measures contraceptive failure per 100 woman-years of exposure. Indicates community-level protection through family planning. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman with a 15-year history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) presents with severe ocular pain, redness, and progressively worsening vision in her left eye for the past 2 weeks. Examination reveals a localized area of scleral thinning with adjacent congestion. There is no posterior involvement on B-scan ultrasound. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: /strong> Explanation: Severe pain, scleral thinning with adjacent congestion are hallmark signs of necrotizing scleritis , the most severe form of RA-associated scleritis. RA leads to immune-mediated vasculitis , causing ischemic necrosis of the sclera . Classification of Scleritis: Anterior Staphyloma (Option A): Anterior staphyloma is a late-stage complication, where uveal tissue bulges through a thinned, scarred sclera. This patient has active inflammation, whereas staphyloma occurs after chronic necrosis and healing. Nodular Scleritis (Option C): Nodular scleritis presents with discrete, firm nodules on the sclera, without necrosis. This patient has scleral thinning and avascular necrosis, which rules out nodular scleritis. Scleromalacia Perforans (Option D): Scleromalacia perforans is a form of necrotizing scleritis WITHOUT inflammation (painless, non-red eye). This patient has severe pain and congestion, so active necrotizing scleritis is the correct choice. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Severe pain, scleral thinning with adjacent congestion are hallmark signs of necrotizing scleritis, the most severe form of RA-associated scleritis.
  • RA leads to immune-mediated vasculitis, causing ischemic necrosis of the sclera.


 

Classification of Scleritis:

 

Anterior Staphyloma (Option A):

  • Anterior staphyloma is a late-stage complication, where uveal tissue bulges through a thinned, scarred sclera.
  • This patient has active inflammation, whereas staphyloma occurs after chronic necrosis and healing.

 

Nodular Scleritis (Option C):

  • Nodular scleritis presents with discrete, firm nodules on the sclera, without necrosis.
  • This patient has scleral thinning and avascular necrosis, which rules out nodular scleritis.

 

Scleromalacia Perforans (Option D):

questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old woman presents with discomfort in her left breast. Mammography reveals a suspicious mass. Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy is performed. Based on the histopathological findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Carcinoma: A subtype of infiltrating ductal carcinoma with Excellent prognosis. Clinical findings: Soft to firm lump due to mucilage. It may be mistaken for a benign tumor. Histopathology: Gross: Soft, shiny, rubbery texture with pale gelatinous/jelly consistency. Microscopy: Tumor cells arranged in clusters or islands with pools of mucin extracellularly and may be intracellularly (called signet ring cell). FNAC: Chicken wire blood vessels (blood vessels get entangled in FNAC needle because of presence of mucin) . ​​​​​​​ Chicken wire blood vessels is also seen in Oligodendroglioma, which is a brain tumor showing fried egg appearance on biopsy and Chicken wire blood vessels. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: In newborns, phytomenadione is routinely administered to prevent hemorrhagic disease. However, its administration is contraindicated in the presence of a deficiency in which specific condition?
questions.stemHtml: In newborns, phytomenadione is routinely administered to prevent hemorrhagic disease. However, its administration is contraindicated in the presence of a deficiency in which specific condition?
questions.solution: Phytomenadione (Vitamin K1) is routinely given to newborns to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn (HDN), which occurs due to Vitamin K deficiency and can cause severe bleeding. However, its administration is contraindicated in newborns with Protein C deficiency, a rare inherited disorder that increases the risk of blood clots. In these infants, Vitamin K can exacerbate clotting, leading to (Purpura fulminans) a life-threatening condition characterized by widespread blood clots and tissue necrosis. But in most cases , as Protein C deficiency would go undiagnosed at birth, Vitamin K birth dose is almost always given. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency (Option A): This genetic disorder affects red blood cells and can lead to hemolytic anemia when exposed to triggers like certain medications. Vitamin K does not cause oxidative stress or hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (Option B): This genetic disorder can lead to lung and liver disease but does not affect the safety of Vitamin K administration in newborns. Cystic fibrosis (Option D): This genetic disorder affects the lungs and digestive system, leading to malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins like Vitamin K. Newborns with cystic fibrosis often need Vitamin K supplementation, making its administration necessary rather than contraindicated. @Neet_pg_bot

NF1 (Neurofibromatosis type 1)

  • Gene: NF1 gene on chromosome 17

  • Protein: Neurofibromin (tumor suppressor)

  • Features:

    • Multiple café-au-lait spots

    • Cutaneous neurofibromas

    • Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas)

    • Optic gliomas

NF2 (Neurofibromatosis type 2)

  • Protein: Merlin (schwannomin)

  • Antoni A and B areas: dense cellular vs loose hypocellular regions

  • Verocay bodies: parallel rows of palisaded nuclei with fibrillary processes between → characteristic of schwannoma

  • S100 positivity: marker of neural crest origin (seen in schwannomas & neurofibromas

questions.stem: A forensic surgeon is examining a stab wound on a victim. Which of the following statement/s is/are true about the dimensions of the wound? 1. Breadth of the wound is equal to the thickness of the weapon. 2. Depth is the greatest dimension of a stab wound. 3. The edges of the wound are clean-cut. 4. The length of the wound is usually slightly less than the width.
questions.stemHtml:
A forensic surgeon is examining a stab wound on a victim. Which of the following statement/s is/are true about the dimensions of the wound?
1. Breadth of the wound is equal to the thickness of the weapon.
2. Depth is the greatest dimension of a stab wound.
3. The edges of the wound are clean-cut.
4. The length of the wound is usually slightly less than the width.
questions.solution: ion: Wound description: when describing a stab wound, it’s important to note the length, width, direction, and appearance of the wound's margins and angles. Margins: The edges of the wound are clean-cut (statement 3) and typically show no abrasion or bruising. In cases of full blade penetration, a patterned abrasion or bruising may occur due to the hilt guard striking the skin. The margins are regular, sharp, and well-defined; however, wounds caused by pointed or conical instruments may have lacerated edges. Length: The length of the wound is usually slightly less than the width (statement 4) of the weapon because of skin stretching. Breadth: The breadth is generally greater than the thickness of the blade (statement 1) due to gaping; proper approximation of the edges is necessary for accurate measurement. Depth: Depth is the greatest dimension of a stab wound (statement 2) and corresponds to the length of the weapon entering the body. If the entire length of the weapon penetrates without producing an exit wound, this depth is critical. Safety note: It is unsafe to determine the depth of a stab wound by probing in the emergency room, as this can disturb any loose clot and lead to severe hemorrhage. Probing may also create a false track by passing between fascial planes or within muscles. Depth assessment should be conducted in the operating theater during wound repair. @Neet_pg_bot

ion:

Wound description: when describing a stab wound, it’s important to note the length, width, direction, and appearance of the wound's margins and angles.

 

Margins:

  • The edges of the wound are clean-cut (statement 3) and typically show no abrasion or bruising.
  • In cases of full blade penetration, a patterned abrasion or bruising may occur due to the hilt guard striking the skin.
  • The margins are regular, sharp, and well-defined; however, wounds caused by pointed or conical instruments may have lacerated edges.

 

Length:

  • The length of the wound is usually slightly less than the width (statement 4) of the weapon because of skin stretching.

 

Breadth:

  • The breadth is generally greater than the thickness of the blade (statement 1) due to gaping; proper approximation of the edges is necessary for accurate measurement.

 

Depth:

  • Depth is the greatest dimension of a stab wound (statement 2) and corresponds to the length of the weapon entering the body.
  • If the entire length of the weapon penetrates without producing an exit wound, this depth is critical.

 

Safety note:

  • It is unsafe to determine the depth of a stab wound by probing in the emergency room, as this can disturb any loose clot and lead to severe hemorrhage.

It reduces intestinal guanylin levels. This results in excessive water and electrolyte secretion into the GIT lumen, leading to secretory diarrhoea. Motilin (Option A): This is involved in stimulating gastric and small intestine motility during fasting. It helps initiate and regulate migratory motor complexes and is not typically influenced by E. coli. Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) (Option C): VIP can induce intestinal water and electrolyte secretion, but it is not specifically targeted by E. coli enterotoxins. VIP-induced diarrhoea is seen in VIPomas. questions.solutionHtml:
Guanylin is the peptide hormone that is influenced by Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC).

  • Guanylin promotes fluid absorption in the small and large intestines.
  • Serum ProGuanylin levels indicate intestinal guanylin levels and reflect intestinal fluid balance.
  • Heat-Stable Enterotoxin of E. coli:
    • Activates guanylyl cyclase enzyme, thus increasing cGMP levels.
    • It reduces intestinal guanylin levels.
    • This results in excessive water and electrolyte secretion into the GIT lumen, leading to secretory diarrhoea.

 

Motilin (Option A): This is involved in stimulating gastric and small intestine motility during fasting. It helps initiate and regulate migratory motor complexes and is not typically influenced by E. coli.

 

Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) (Option C): VIP can induce intestinal water and electrolyte secretion, but it is not specifically targeted by E. coli enterotoxins. VIP-induced diarrhoea is seen in VIPomas.

 

Calcitonin gene receptor peptide (CGRP) (Option D): CGRP is involved in somatostatin release, which is an inhibitor of GIT secretion; it also causes smooth muscle contraction

questions.stem: A 35-year-old pregnant woman is being assessed for suspected appendicitis. An abdominal ultrasound shows inflammation but in limited detail. What is the best contrast agent to enhance USG?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old pregnant woman is being assessed for suspected appendicitis. An abdominal ultrasound shows inflammation but in limited detail. What is the best contrast agent to enhance USG?
questions.solution: Correct Answer: D) Sulfur Hexafluoride microbubbles In contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS), microbubbles or microspheres , such as those found in Sonovist and Levovist , contain sulfur hexafluoride gas encapsulated in a phospholipid shell. These microbubbles improve the visualization of blood flow and enhance the imaging of vascular structures and lesions. Another type of microbubble in CEUS consists of octafluoropropane gas within a phospholipid shell. Contrast agents for USG Examples Sonovue (sulfur hexafluoride) Lumason (sulfur hexafluoride) Definity (perflutren) Sonozoid (perflubutane) Preferred route Intravenous Eliminated by Lungs (hence safe in Renal conditions) Indications Liver lesions Micturating cystosonography Renal lesions Obstruction in Crohn's disease Evaluation of Aortic aneurysm repair Adverse Effects It is the safest contrast media and rarely causes mild anaphylactoid reactions. Barium sulfate (Option A) is the most commonly used contrast agent for identifying gastrointestinal tract issues such as ulcers, tumours, strictures, or inflammation. It is not water-soluble and is given orally or rectally. Iodinated contrast agents (Option B) are water-soluble and are widely used for X-rays, CT scans, and interventional radiology. However, they are highly nephrotoxic and should be used with caution in patients with renal impairment only after evaluating renal function. Saline solution (Option C) enhances the visualisation of internal structures, such as in saline infusion sonohysterography and hysterosalpingo-contrast sonography, which is mixed with air to improve the visibility of fallopian tubes and identify peritoneal spills. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer: D) Sulfur Hexafluoride microbubbles

  • In contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS), microbubbles or microspheres, such as those found in Sonovist and Levovist, contain sulfur hexafluoride gas encapsulated in a phospholipid shell.
  • These microbubbles improve the visualization of blood flow and enhance the imaging of vascular structures and lesions.
  • Another type of microbubble in CEUS consists of octafluoropropane gas within a phospholipid shell.

 

Contrast agents for USG

Examples
  • Sonovue (sulfur hexafluoride)
  • Lumason (sulfur hexafluoride)
  • Definity (perflutren)
  • Sonozoid (perflubutane)

Preferred route

Intravenous

Eliminated by

Lungs (hence safe in Renal conditions)

Indications
  • Liver lesions
  • Micturating cystosonography
  • Renal lesions
  • Obstruction in Crohn's disease
  • Evaluation of Aortic aneurysm repair

Adverse Effects

It is the safest contrast media and rarely causes mild anaphylactoid reactions.


 

Barium sulfate (Option A) is the most commonly used contrast agent for identifying gastrointestinal tract issues such as ulcers, tumours, strictures, or inflammation. It is not water-soluble and is given orally or rectally.

 

Iodinated contrast agents (Option B) are water-soluble and are widely used for X-rays, CT scans, and interventional radiology. However, they are highly nephrotoxic and should be used with caution in patients with renal impairment only after evaluating renal function.


Saline solution (Option C) enhances the visualisation of internal structures, such as in saline infusion sonohysterography and hysterosalpingo-contrast sonography, which is mixed with air to improve the visibility of fallopian tubes and identify peritoneal spills.

questions.stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl presents with early breast development and pubic hair growth. Which among the following investigations can differentiate between central and peripheral causes of precocious puberty?
questions.solution: Explanation: The GnRH stimulation test is used to differentiate between central and peripheral causes. 100 µg of GnRH is adminis­tered (SC), and the serum level of LH is measured. A Value Of LH >15 mIU/mL suggests gonadotropin-dependent (central) precocious puberty. In Central Precocious Puberty, GnRH stimulation significantly increases LH and FSH levels, resulting in elevated estrogen levels. In Peripheral Precocious Puberty, these levels will not increase significantly because of negative feedback by the exogenously produced estrogen. Negative feedback on LH and FSH Due to: Elevated estrogen: Isosexual Elevated androgen: Heterosexual Causes: 90% idiopathic 10% brain tumor (hamartoma of tuber cinerum) Always do an MRI scan Causes: Elevated estrogen Granulosa cell tumor Hypothyroidism (Alpha subunit similar to LH and FSH). McCune Albright syndrome Elevated androgen Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor (androgen-secreting tumor of ovary) CAH (Congenital adrenal hyperplasia) Basic investigations in precocious puberty: Serum hCG, FSH, LH, and prolactin (A baseline prepubertal LH level of greater than 0.3 IU/L is suggestive of Central Precocious Puberty). Thyroid profile (TSH, T4). Serum estradiol, testosterone, 17-OH progesterone, DHEA. USG, CT, or MRI of the abdomen and pelvis to rule out pathology of ovaries, adrenals, or uterus. Skull X-ray, CT scan, or MRI brain—to exclude intracranial lesions (hypothalamic hamartoma). Electroencephalogram (EEG): Abnormal EEG is often associated with CNS disease. X-ray hand and wrist (nondominant) for bone age. GnRH stimulation test Bone age assessment (Option A): In cases of precocious puberty, bone age is usually advanced beyond the child's chronological age, indicating early hormonal influence on bone growth. However, it does not differentiate between central and peripheral precocious puberty. Pelvic ultrasound (Option B): It can identify ovarian cysts or tumours that might be responsible for peripheral precocious puberty, but it only rules out ovarian pathologies. Serum estradiol levels (Option D) : It does not differentiate between central and peripheral causes of precocious puberty. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

The GnRH stimulation test is used to differentiate between central and peripheral causes. 100 µg of GnRH is adminis­tered (SC), and the serum level of LH is measured. A Value Of LH >15 mIU/mL suggests gonadotropin-dependent (central) precocious puberty.

  • In Central Precocious Puberty, GnRH stimulation significantly increases LH and FSH levels, resulting in elevated estrogen levels.
  • In Peripheral Precocious Puberty, these levels will not increase significantly because of negative feedback by the exogenously produced estrogen.

Central (True precocious puberty)

Peripheral precocious puberty
  • Premature activation of the HPO axis
  • Elevated LH (diagnostic)
  • Elevated FSH (diagnostic)
  • Elevated estrogen
  • Due to an increase in estrogen, puberty is always isosexual
  • Due to the exogenous production of estrogen
  • Isolated elevated estrogen and elevated androgen.
  • Negative feedback on LH and FSH
  • Due to:
    • Elevated estrogen: Isosexual
    • Elevated androgen: Heterosexual

Causes:

  • 90% idiopathic
  • 10% brain tumor (hamartoma of tuber cinerum)

Always do an MRI scan

Causes:

  • Elevated estrogen
    • Granulosa cell tumor
    • Hypothyroidism (Alpha subunit similar to LH and FSH).
    • McCune Albright syndrome
  • Elevated androgen
    • Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor (androgen-secreting tumor of ovary)
    • CAH (Congenital adrenal hyperplasia)

 

Basic investigations in precocious puberty:

  • Serum hCG, FSH, LH, and prolactin (A baseline prepubertal LH level of greater than 0.3 IU/L is suggestive of Central Precocious Puberty).
  • Thyroid profile (TSH, T4).
  • Serum estradiol, testosterone, 17-OH progesterone, DHEA.
  • USG, CT, or MRI of the abdomen and pelvis to rule out pathology of ovaries, adrenals, or uterus.
  • Skull X-ray, CT scan, or MRI brain—to exclude intracranial lesions (hypothalamic hamartoma).
  • Electroencephalogram (EEG): Abnormal EEG is often associated with CNS disease.
  • X-ray hand and wrist (nondominant) for bone age.
  • GnRH stimulation test

Bone age assessment (Option A): In cases of precocious puberty, bone age is usually advanced beyond the child's chronological age, indicating early hormonal influence on bone growth. However, it does not differentiate between central and peripheral precocious puberty.
 

Pelvic ultrasound (Option B): It can identify ovarian cysts or tumours that might be responsible for peripheral precocious puberty, but it only rules out ovarian pathologies.
 

Serum estradiol levels (Option D): It does not differentiate between central and peripheral causes of precocious puberty.

Several conditions must be evaluated and met before deciding to proceed with the diagnosis of brain death.

questions.stem: Which stimulation pattern is specifically designed to assess deep neuromuscular blockade?
questions.stemHtml: Which stimulation pattern is specifically designed to assess deep neuromuscular blockade?
questions.solution: ount (PTC) stimulation is used to assess deep levels of neuromuscular blockade that are not detectable by TOF stimulation. Patterns of Nerve Stimulation for the evaluation of the neuromuscular function: Stimulation Pattern Mechanism Interpretation Clinical Implication and Limitation Single-Twitch Stimulation (Option B) Single electrical stimulus applied at a frequency of 0.1 Hz to 1 Hz. Requires comparison to pre-NMBA administration value. Muscle response to the stimulus reflects neuromuscular block onset; changes in twitch height help assess blockade. Used to evaluate onset of neuromuscular block. Limited utility as a standalone test. Train-of-Four (TOF) Stimulation (Option A) Four supramaximal stimuli delivered at 0.5-second intervals (2 Hz). Fade between responses indicates degree of block. TOF count assesses onset . TOF ratio measures recovery . Fade suggests nondepolarizing block. Most common pattern for intraoperative monitoring. Cannot measure deep block or phase I block. Double-Burst Stimulation (DBS) (Option D) Two bursts of 50-Hz stimulation with a 750-ms interval. Fade between the two bursts indicates block. Fade between bursts correlates with TOF ratio. DBS is more sensitive for detecting fade. Better tactile detection of residual block than TOF but cannot reliably assess recovery at higher TOF ratios. Tetanic Stimulation High-frequency stimulation (50-100 Hz for 5 seconds) causing sustained muscle contraction . Fade indicates nondepolarizing block; sustained response suggests normal transmission or depolarizing block. Painful and limited use in practice. May cause lasting muscle antagonism, affecting recovery assessment. Post Tetanic Count (PTC) Stimulation (Option C) Tetanic stimulation (50 Hz for 5 seconds) followed by single twitches at 1 Hz after 3 seconds. Counts discernible twitches after tetanic stimulation; assesses deep block not detectable by TOF. Used for monitoring deep neuromuscular blockade. Requires 6-minute intervals, limiting continuous use. @Neet_pg_bot

s="customMeta" data-dictid="5b9831f3aa169277718395d7361df6">bone marrow aspirate and splenic aspirate are 3 important investigations done for the diagnosis of kala-azar.

 

Diagnosis of Kala-azar :

 

Microscopy

Demonstration of amastigotes in smears of tissue aspirates is the gold standard for diagnosis of kala-azar / VL

 

Materials collected:

Peripheral blood smear: Peripheral blood contains the amastigotes present inside circulating monocytes. It is best to examine buffy coat smear, Buffy coat smears show a diurnal periodicity, more smears being positive when collected during the day than at night.

 

Blood smear test showing macrophages with amastigotes and extracellular Leishmania parasites (white arrows)

 

Bone marrow aspirate: shows Leishmania donovani bodies (LD bodies) in macrophages characterised by a kinetoplast and characteristic double dot appearance (Fig. A and B).

Splenic aspirate (most sensitive): Splenic aspirates are richer in parasites and, therefore, are more valuable for diagnosis. Splenic aspiration is contraindicated in patients with prolonged prothrombin time or if platelet count is less than 40,000/mm³

Serodiagnosis
  1. Detection of antigen: ELISA and PCR
  2. Detection of antibody:
    • rk39 test: A specific rapid immunochromatographic test (ICT) method for antibodies using a recombinant leishmanial antigen rk 39. The sensitivity of the test is 98% and specificity is 90%.
    • Complement fixation test
    • Indirect immunofluorescent antibody test (IFAT)
    • Counter immunoelectrophoresis (CIEP)
    • ELISA and DOT-ELISA
    • Direct agglutination test (DAT)


Liver biopsy is not a safe procedure and carries a risk of haemorrhage.

  • The ones with a lower CT number appear the darkest, and the ones with a higher CT number appear brighter.

style="border-collapse:collapse; width:631px">

VARICELLA VACCINE

About Vaccine

  • Live-attenuated vaccine
  • Oka strain

Dose, Route & Site

  • 0.5 mL, Subcutaneously
  • Anterolateral thigh or upper arm

National Program

Not included

IAP 2021

  • All children, especially high-risk categories; those exposed to varicella, and exposed unvaccinated adolescents/adults.
  • The first dose is taken at 15-18 months (minimum age 12 months).
  • Second dose 3-6 months later.

Catch Up

Administer two doses ≥3 months apart (≥4 weeks apart if over 13 years old) for those without proof of immunity.

Post-exposure prophylaxis

When administered for PEP within 72 hours of contact, a single dose of the vaccine offers only about 70% protective efficacy.

Adverse Reactions

  • Fever, rash, local pain or redness.
  • Mild rash after 2-3 weeks (5%).

C/I

  • The IAP advises against administering the MMR-V vaccine to children under 2 years old.
  • Anaphylaxis after the previous dose
  • Immunodeficiency
  • Active leukaemia or lymphoma
  • During immunosuppressive therapy

Precautions

  • Moderate to severe illness
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • Recent receipt of blood products or immunoglobulins
  • Therapy with aspirin

Storage

  • Freeze-dried, lyophilized; Store at 2-8°C; Protect from light.
  • Use within 30 minutes of reconstitution.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is undergoing evaluation for palpitations. ECG reveals a supraventricular tachycardia with HR of 190/min. An echocardiogram reveals hypertrophy of the right ventricle and enlargement of the right ventricular outflow tract. Which structure separates the inflow and outflow tracts in the right ventricle?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man is undergoing evaluation for palpitations. ECG reveals a supraventricular tachycardia with HR of 190/min. An echocardiogram reveals hypertrophy of the right ventricle and enlargement of the right ventricular outflow tract. Which structure separates the inflow and outflow tracts in the right ventricle?
questions.solution: p> The supraventricular crest is located within the right ventricle and separates the inflow tract , which carries blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve, from the outflow tract, which directs blood into the pulmonary trunk. It is a thick, muscular “U” shaped structure extending from the interventricular septum to the anterolateral wall of the right ventricle. The crest provides the main attachment for the anterosuperior leaflet of the tricuspid valve. The septal limb of the crest is connected to the septal limbs of the septomarginal trabeculation (moderator band). Crista terminalis (Option A) Located in the right atrium - separates the smooth and rough parts of the atrium, not the right ventricle's inflow and outflow tracts. The moderator band (Option C) facilitates conduction in the right ventricle and contains the right bundle branch (RBB) . Helps prevent overdistension of the right ventricle during systole by acting as a stabilizing structure. It does not separate the inflow and outflow regions. Interventricular septum (Option D) separates the left and right ventricles but does not partition the right ventricle's inflow and outflow tracts. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
p>

The supraventricular crest is located within the right ventricle and separates the inflow tract, which carries blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve, from the outflow tract, which directs blood into the pulmonary trunk.

  • It is a thick, muscular “U” shaped structure extending from the interventricular septum to the anterolateral wall of the right ventricle.
  • The crest provides the main attachment for the anterosuperior leaflet of the tricuspid valve.
  • The septal limb of the crest is connected to the septal limbs of the septomarginal trabeculation (moderator band).

    

Crista terminalis (Option A)

  • Located in the right atrium - separates the smooth and rough parts of the atrium, not the right ventricle's inflow and outflow tracts.

 

The moderator band (Option C) facilitates conduction in the right ventricle and contains the right bundle branch (RBB).

  • Helps prevent overdistension of the right ventricle during systole by acting as a stabilizing structure. It does not separate the inflow and outflow regions.

 

Interventricular septum (Option D) separates the left and right ventricles but does not partition the right ventricle's inflow and outflow tracts.

questions.stem: All of the following criteria are used for diagnosing PCOS except?
questions.stemHtml: All of the following criteria are used for diagnosing PCOS except?
questions.solution: p> Explanation: Elevated estrogen levels can occur in some cases of PCOS due to disturbances in hormone regulation, it is not a primary diagnostic criterion for PCOS. Rotterdam Criteria: Any 2 of the following 3 should be present to make a provisional diagnosis for PCOS Increased androgen levels (Option A): Hyperandrogenism/Hirsutism: PCOS is associated with elevated androgen levels, which can manifest as clinical signs (like hirsutism and acne) or biochemical findings (elevated testosterone). Ovulatory dysfunction (Option B): Oligomenorrhea/Amenorrhea- Irregular menstrual cycles (oligomenorrhea) or absence of menstrual periods (amenorrhea) are common features of PCOS due to ovulatory dysfunction. Presence of ovarian cysts (Option D): On USG: 1 or both ovaries >12 follicles with 2-9mm in size (<1cm)- One of the diagnostic criteria for PCOS is the presence of polycystic ovarian morphology, which is confirmed by ultrasound showing multiple cysts on the ovaries. USG : Necklace pattern arranged towards the periphery. @Neet_pg_bot

p>

Explanation:

Elevated estrogen levels can occur in some cases of PCOS due to disturbances in hormone regulation, it is not a primary diagnostic criterion for PCOS.

Rotterdam Criteria:

Any 2 of the following 3 should be present to make a provisional diagnosis for PCOS

Increased androgen levels (Option A): Hyperandrogenism/Hirsutism: PCOS is associated with elevated androgen levels, which can manifest as clinical signs (like hirsutism and acne) or biochemical findings (elevated testosterone).

Ovulatory dysfunction (Option B): Oligomenorrhea/Amenorrhea- Irregular menstrual cycles (oligomenorrhea) or absence of menstrual periods (amenorrhea) are common features of PCOS due to ovulatory dysfunction.

Presence of ovarian cysts (Option D): On USG: 1 or both ovaries >12 follicles with 2-9mm in size (<1cm)- One of the diagnostic criteria for PCOS is the presence of polycystic ovarian morphology, which is confirmed by ultrasound showing multiple cysts on the ovaries.

USG: Necklace pattern arranged towards the periphery.

questions.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of palpable purpura on her lower legs, no systemic symptoms, and all investigations including ANA, ANCA, and complements are normal. Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

  • Radiographic Findings of Hydatid Cyst:
    • Uncomplicated cysts appear as thin-walled, round or oval masses with low-attenuation contents and a thin enhancing wall, up to 10 cm in size.

 

  • Signs of Impending Rupture:
    • Meniscus Sign: Air lucency between the pericyst and laminated membranes when cyst communicates with bronchioles. (Option A)
  • Signs Associated with Cyst Rupture:
    • Cumbo Sign or Onion Peel Sign:
      • Indicates that the endocyst has shrunk and ruptured due to increasing air.

    • Water Lily Sign:
      • Also known as the camalote sign.
      • Indicates that the endocyst membrane is detached; it will appear as a floating curvilinear structure (fluid-filled cyst ) within an intact pericyst.
      • This gives the appearance of a floating water lily. (Option C)
    • Mass Within the Cavity: An endocyst floating in a completely fluid-filled cyst.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presents with fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance. On physical examination, she has diffuse goitre and dry skin. questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old female presents with fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance. On physical examination, she has diffuse goitre and dry skin. Histopathological examination shows lymphoid infiltration, atrophic thyroid follicles lined in many areas by epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm as shown below. What is the likely diagnosis? {{caption_text}}
questions.solution: and HPE findings suggest a diagnosis of Hashimoto's thyroiditis/Lymphocytic thyroiditis.. It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas. In histopathology, there is extensive lymphocytic infiltration with well-developed germinal centres. The thyroid follicles are atrophic and are lined in many areas by epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm, termed Hürthle cells (hallmark feature of Hashimoto's thyroiditis) . It is an autoimmune condition, so on hematological testing we see autoantibodies like Anti-TSH receptor antibody, antithyroglobulin antibody, and anti-TPO antibodies. Genetic cause of Hashimoto's thyroiditis is HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR5 polymorphisms. Long standing Hashimoto's thyroiditis can give rise to some cancers like: Papillary carcinoma thyroid Maltoma (a marginal zone lymphoma) {{caption_text}} @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 5-month-old boy presents with failure to thrive, developmental delay, and intermittent episodes of vomiting and lethargy. The episodes coincide with the introduction of solid foods. Blood tests reveal elevated ammonia levels and high levels of ornithine in blood. Urine analysis shows increased excretion of homocitrulline. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 5-month-old boy presents with failure to thrive, developmental delay, and intermittent episodes of vomiting and lethargy. The episodes coincide with the introduction of solid foods. Blood tests reveal elevated ammonia levels and high levels of ornithine in blood. Urine analysis shows increased excretion of homocitrulline. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.solution: This child with hyperammonemia triggered after solid food introduction is most likely to have HHH syndrome. Hyperornithinemia-Hyperammonemia-Homocitrullinuria Syndrome Inheritance Autosomal recessive Defective Gene ORC1 Defective Protein Mitochondrial Ornithine Transporter: This transporter moves ornithine into the mitochondria and citrulline out of the mitochondria. Mechanism Prevents ornithine from entering the mitochondria, which is necessary for the urea cycle. The buildup of ammonia in the blood (hyperammonemia). Ornithine also accumulates in the cytoplasm (hyperornithinemia). Carbamoyl phosphate reacts with lysine to form homocitrulline. Symptoms Failure to thrive. Developmental delay. Intermittent episodes of vomiting and lethargy (triggered by protein intake). Seizures. Intellectual disability. Diagnosis Elevated blood ammonia Elevated blood ornithine Elevated urinary homocitrulline. Treatment Low-protein diet Nitrogen scavenger medications Liver transplant in severe cases. Citrullinemia (Option A) leads to the accumulation of citrulline, which would be elevated in blood tests, unlike in this scenario. Argininosuccinate aciduria (Option B) causes the characteristic symptom of trichorrhexis nodosa (brittle, easily broken hair), which is not mentioned in this scenario. Argininemia (Option D) involves hyperammonemia . Compared to other urea cycle disorders, its presentation is typically delayed, appearing around 2 years of age, not at 5 months. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
This child with hyperammonemia triggered after solid food introduction is most likely to have HHH syndrome.

 

Hyperornithinemia-Hyperammonemia-Homocitrullinuria Syndrome

Inheritance

Autosomal recessive

Defective Gene

ORC1

Defective Protein

Mitochondrial Ornithine Transporter: This transporter moves ornithine into the mitochondria and citrulline out of the mitochondria.

Mechanism
  • Prevents ornithine from entering the mitochondria, which is necessary for the urea cycle.
  • The buildup of ammonia in the blood (hyperammonemia).
  • Ornithine also accumulates in the cytoplasm (hyperornithinemia).
  • Carbamoyl phosphate reacts with lysine to form homocitrulline.

Symptoms
  • Failure to thrive.
  • Developmental delay.
  • Intermittent episodes of vomiting and lethargy (triggered by protein intake).
  • Seizures.
  • Intellectual disability.

Diagnosis
  • Elevated blood ammonia
  • Elevated blood ornithine
  • Elevated urinary homocitrulline.

Treatment
  • Low-protein diet
  • Nitrogen scavenger medications
  • Liver transplant in severe cases.

 

  • Citrullinemia (Option A) leads to the accumulation of citrulline, which would be elevated in blood tests, unlike in this scenario.

 

  • Argininosuccinate aciduria (Option B) causes the characteristic symptom of trichorrhexis nodosa (brittle, easily broken hair), which is not mentioned in this scenario.

 

  • Argininemia (Option D) involves hyperammonemia. Compared to other urea cycle disorders, its presentation is typically delayed, appearing around 2 years of age, not at 5 months.

questions.solution: Phases of translation Key events Initiation Dissociation of 80s ribosome into 60s and 40s, and stabilized by various initiation factors. Formation of the 43S Preinitiation Complex: The 40S ribosomal subunit, in association with initiation factors, binds to the initiator tRNA (carrying methionine in eukaryotes or formyl-methionine in prokaryotes)forming the 43S preinitiation complex. Formation of 48S initiation complex: The 43S complex binds to the 5' end of the mRNA, and scans for start codon which upon recognition, the 48S initiation complex is formed. Formation of the 80S Initiation Complex: Binding of the 60S ribosomal subunit to the 48S initiation. The met-tRNA on the P site of the ribosome is ready for the elongation cycle. Elongation Binding of Aminoacyl-tRNA to the A Site Peptide Bond Formation Elongation factor 2 (EF2) binds to and displaces the peptidyl tRNA from the A site to the P site Termination Ribosome reaches the terminator codon sequence (UAA, UAG or UGA) Releasing factor(RF1), (RF3) and GTP complex promotes hydrolysis releasing the protein and the tRNA from the P site. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Phases of translation

Key events

Initiation
  • Dissociation of 80s ribosome into 60s and 40s, and stabilized by various initiation factors.
  • Formation of the 43S Preinitiation Complex: The 40S ribosomal subunit, in association with initiation factors, binds to the initiator tRNA (carrying methionine in eukaryotes or formyl-methionine in prokaryotes)forming the 43S preinitiation complex.
  • Formation of 48S initiation complex: The 43S complex binds to the 5' end of the mRNA, and scans for start codon which upon recognition, the 48S initiation complex is formed.
  • Formation of the 80S Initiation Complex: Binding of the 60S ribosomal subunit to the 48S initiation. The met-tRNA on the P site of the ribosome is ready for the elongation cycle.

Elongation
  • Binding of Aminoacyl-tRNA to the A Site
  • Peptide Bond Formation
  • Elongation factor 2 (EF2) binds to and displaces the peptidyl tRNA from the A site to the P site

Termination
  • Ribosome reaches the terminator codon sequence (UAA, UAG or UGA)
  • Releasing factor(RF1), (RF3) and GTP complex promotes hydrolysis releasing the protein and the tRNA from the P site.

questions.stem: A patient is given a 300 mg dose of a drug. After 1 hour, 75 mg of the drug is excreted. Assuming the drug is eliminated from the system by following first-order kinetics, how much of the drug will remain after 4 hours of starting the drug?
questions.stemHtml: A patient is given a 300 mg dose of a drug. After 1 hour, 75 mg of the drug is excreted. Assuming the drug is eliminated from the system by following first-order kinetics, how much of the drug will remain after 4 hours of starting the drug?
questions.solution: anation The given drug follows a first-order kinetic elimination; hence, its clearance rate remains constant and proportional to the plasma concentration per unit of time. Initial dose: 300 mg After 1 hour: 75 mg excreted So, 225 mg remains → this means 75% (¾) remains after 1 hour Drug follows first-order kinetics , so the fraction eliminated per unit time remains constant Therefore, the remaining drug after each hour is: After 1 hour: 300×3/4=225 mg After 2 hours: 225×3/4=168.75 mg After 3 hours: 168.75×3/4=126.56 mg After 4 hours: 126.56×3/4= 94.92 mg @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
anation

The given drug follows a first-order kinetic elimination; hence, its clearance rate remains constant and proportional to the plasma concentration per unit of time.

  • Initial dose: 300 mg

  • After 1 hour: 75 mg excreted

  • So, 225 mg remains → this means 75% (¾) remains after 1 hour

  • Drug follows first-order kinetics, so the fraction eliminated per unit time remains constant

Therefore, the remaining drug after each hour is:

  • After 1 hour:
    300×3/4=225 mg

  • After 2 hours:
    225×3/4=168.75 mg

  • After 3 hours:
    168.75×3/4=126.56 mg

  • After 4 hours:
    126.56×3/4=94.92 mg

questions.stemHtml: A 58-year-old male with a 20-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and an HbA1c of 10.5% came for an ophthalmic examination. Fundoscopy reveals microaneurysms, hard exudates, and retinal thickening. Which of the following is the most likely cause of future vision loss in this patient?
questions.solution: lanation: The most likely cause of future vision loss in this patient is macular edema. Complications of Diabetic Retinopathy: Macular Edema: The most common cause of vision loss in diabetic retinopathy is leakage from dilated capillaries. Vitreous Hemorrhage (VH) (Option A): Seen as blood floating in the vitreous, occluding the view of the retina. Secondary to proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) is a cause of severe vision loss in diabetic patients Retinal Detachment (Option B): PDR causes scars to form in the back of the eye. When the scars pull the retina away from the back of the eye, it's called tractional retinal detachment. Neovascular Glaucoma (Option D): PDR causes abnormal blood vessels to grow out of the retina and block fluid from draining out of the eye, leading to neovascular glaucoma. Can cause vision loss and blindness. Rubeosis Iridis: Neovascularization of the iris is when blood vessels develop on the anterior surface of the iris in response to retinal ischemia. Prone to spontaneous hyphema as the blood vessels are fragile @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
lanation: 

The most likely cause of future vision loss in this patient is macular edema. 

 Complications of Diabetic Retinopathy:

  • Macular Edema: The most common cause of vision loss in diabetic retinopathy is leakage from dilated capillaries.

 

  • Vitreous Hemorrhage (VH) (Option A): Seen as blood floating in the vitreous, occluding the view of the retina. Secondary to proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) is a cause of severe vision loss in diabetic patients

 

  • Retinal Detachment (Option B): PDR causes scars to form in the back of the eye. When the scars pull the retina away from the back of the eye, it's called tractional retinal detachment.

 

  • Neovascular Glaucoma (Option D): PDR causes abnormal blood vessels to grow out of the retina and block fluid from draining out of the eye, leading to neovascular glaucoma. Can cause vision loss and blindness.

 

  • Rubeosis Iridis: Neovascularization of the iris is when blood vessels develop on the anterior surface of the iris in response to retinal ischemia. Prone to spontaneous hyphema as the blood vessels are fragile

Explanation:

Stages of spore formation/sporulation in order:

  1. Axial filament formation: The bacterial cell prepares for sporulation by forming an axial filament.
  2. Septum formation: Under stress (e.g., nutrient depletion), the bacterium divides asymmetrically, forming a septum that separates the mother cell from the forespore.
  3. Asymmetric division: The smaller compartment forms the forespore (future spore), while the larger one becomes the mother cell.
  4. Engulfment: The mother cell engulfs the forespore within a second membrane.
  5. Cortex formation: A thick layer of peptidoglycan forms between the two membranes of the spore.
  6. Coat formation: Various proteins assemble around the spore, forming the coat.
  7. Maturation: The spore matures, becoming highly resistant to environmental stresses.
  8. Lysis: The mother cell lyses, releasing the mature spore into the environment.

questions.solution: The peripheral smear findings can help distinguish between different types of thalassemia: β-thalassemia major (Patient A): This condition is characterized by severe anemia . The peripheral smear typically shows significant abnormalities, including target cells , nucleated red blood cells (NRBCs) , microcytosis, hypochromia, and anisopoikilocytosis. These findings are consistent with the severe hemolytic anemia and ineffective erythropoiesis seen in β-thalassemia major. β-thalassemia minor/β-thalassemia trait (Patient B): This condition usually presents with mild anemia. The peripheral smear shows microcytosis and hypochromia but generally lacks significant numbers of NRBCs. α-thalassemia (Patient C): This condition can vary in severity. The peripheral smear of a patient with α-thalassemia trait may show mild anemia , microcytosis, and hypochromia. In cases of HbH disease (a form of α-thalassemia), the smear can also show NRBCs and hemoglobin H inclusions (golf ball cells), which are not seen in β-thalassemia minor. Hemoglobin H inclusions are seen in α-thalassemia patients when there are 3 out of 4 alpha genes deletions. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
The peripheral smear findings can help distinguish between different types of thalassemia:

  • β-thalassemia major (Patient A): This condition is characterized by severe anemia. The peripheral smear typically shows significant abnormalities, including target cells, nucleated red blood cells (NRBCs), microcytosis, hypochromia, and anisopoikilocytosis. These findings are consistent with the severe hemolytic anemia and ineffective erythropoiesis seen in β-thalassemia major.
  • β-thalassemia minor/β-thalassemia trait (Patient B): This condition usually presents with mild anemia. The peripheral smear shows microcytosis and hypochromia but generally lacks significant numbers of NRBCs.
  • α-thalassemia (Patient C): This condition can vary in severity. The peripheral smear of a patient with α-thalassemia trait may show mild anemia, microcytosis, and hypochromia. In cases of HbH disease (a form of α-thalassemia), the smear can also show NRBCs and hemoglobin H inclusions (golf ball cells), which are not seen in β-thalassemia minor.
    • Hemoglobin H inclusions are seen in α-thalassemia patients when there are 3 out of 4 alpha genes deletions.

questions.solution: he antihypertensive medications of choice in all children with pediatric CKD as they decrease BP as well as proteinuria. Treatment of Pediatric CKD: Nutrition Management Dietary Protein restriction is not suggested. Children with CKD stage 2-5 should receive 100% of the daily reference intake of vitamins and minerals. Blood Pressure Control Antihypertensive drugs, like ACE inhibitors or ARBs, are often prescribed to manage high BP. Anemia Treatment Erythropoietin-stimulating agents (ESAs) or iron supplements. Phosphate Binders (Calcium carbonate, calcium acetate, Sevelamer, Ferric citrate) to maintain normal serum calcium and phosphorus levels. Ergocalciferol or Cholecalciferol Typically recommended to treat insufficient 25OH vitamin D Bicitra or Sodium Bicarbonate tablets Used to maintain the serum bicarbonate levels > 22mEq/L. Recombinant human growth hormone(rHuGH) Given by daily subcutaneous injections and continues until the patient reaches the 50 th percentile for mid-parental height. Dialysis and Kidney Transplantation Preferred treatment for children with end-stage renal disease. Vaccinations Special considerations for immunocompromised children. questions.solutionHtml:
he antihypertensive medications of choice in all children with pediatric CKD as they decrease BP as well as proteinuria.

 

Treatment of Pediatric CKD: 

 

Nutrition Management
  • Dietary Protein restriction is not suggested.
  • Children with CKD stage 2-5 should receive 100% of the daily reference intake of vitamins and minerals.

Blood Pressure Control
  • Antihypertensive drugs, like ACE inhibitors or ARBs, are often prescribed to manage high BP.

Anemia Treatment
  • Erythropoietin-stimulating agents (ESAs) or iron supplements.

Phosphate Binders
  • (Calcium carbonate, calcium acetate, Sevelamer, Ferric citrate) to maintain normal serum calcium and phosphorus levels.

Ergocalciferol or Cholecalciferol
  • Typically recommended to treat insufficient 25OH vitamin D

Bicitra or Sodium Bicarbonate tablets
  • Used to maintain the serum bicarbonate levels > 22mEq/L.

Recombinant human growth hormone(rHuGH)
  • Given by daily subcutaneous injections and continues until the patient reaches the 50th percentile for mid-parental height.

Dialysis and Kidney Transplantation
  • Preferred treatment for children with end-stage renal disease.

Vaccinations
  • Special considerations for immunocompromised children.

 

  • Metoprolol (Option A), Amlodipine (Option B) & Furosemide (Option D): They do not have the added benefit of reducing proteinuria or slowing the progression of CKD.

Hermansky–Pudlak syndrome (HPS) is a rare, autosomal recessive form of oculocutaneous albinism and non-pigmented symptoms such as bleeding diathesis . It is caused by mutations in genes encoding components of specific protein complexes involved in lysosome biogenesis and trafficking. These mutations lead to impaired melanosome maturation and the absence of dense bodies in platelets. Common manifestations across HPS subtypes include reduced pigmentation in the eyes, hair, and skin, along with easy bruising, bleeding tendencies, interstitial pulmonary fibrosis , and granulomatous colitis in severe cases. Option B: Weibel-Palade bodies are secretory granules found in endothelial cells and are involved in regulating vascular function. Dysregulation of Weibel-Palade bodies can result in impaired hemostasis, endothelial dysfunction, and a high risk of thrombus formation. Hermansky–Pudlak syndrome (HPS) is a rare, autosomal recessive form of oculocutaneous albinism and non-pigmented symptoms such as bleeding diathesis. 

It is caused by mutations in genes encoding components of specific protein complexes involved in lysosome biogenesis and trafficking. These mutations lead to impaired melanosome maturation and the absence of dense bodies in platelets.

Common manifestations across HPS subtypes include reduced pigmentation in the eyes, hair, and skin, along with easy bruising, bleeding tendencies, interstitial pulmonary fibrosis, and granulomatous colitis in severe cases.

Platelet granule defects: 
Alpha granule defect- Grey platelet syndrome
Delta granule defect- Hermansky Pudlak syndrome

OTHER OPTIONS:

Option A: Ceroid lipofuscin accumulation is observed in abnormal lysosomes of various organs in HPS, including alveolar macrophages in the lungs, it is not primarily associated with epidermal cells in the skin.

Option B: Weibel-Palade bodies are secretory granules found in endothelial cells and are involved in regulating vascular function. Dysregulation of Weibel-Palade bodies can result in impaired hemostasis, endothelial dysfunction, and a high risk of thrombus formation.

Option D: Autophagocytosis and defective fission of large melanosomes are seen in Chediak-Higashi syndrome, which occurs due to a loss-of-function mutation in the LYST gene (lysosomal trafficking regulator/CHS 1).

    • 1 Major Manifestation plus 2 Minor Manifestations

     

    Modified Jones Criteria for Diagnosing Rheumatic Fever

    Historical Background:

    • Original Jones criteria established in 1944.
    • Significant updates in 1992 and later.

    Key Components:

    Criteria Type

    Components

    Major Criteria
    1. Carditis (Option D)
    2. Polyarthritis
    3. Chorea
    4. Erythema marginatum
    5. Subcutaneous nodules

    Minor Criteria
    1. Fever (Option C ruled out)
    2. Arthralgia (Option A ruled out)
    3. Elevated acute phase reactants (e.g., ESR, CRP) (Option B ruled out)
    4. Prolonged PR interval on ECG

    Major Criteria

    Low-risk Population

    • Carditis (clinical or subclinical)
    • Arthritis (polyarthritis only)
    • Chorea
    • Erythema marginatum
    • Subcutaneous nodule

    Moderate- to High-risk Population

    • Carditis (clinical or subclinical)
    • Arthritis (polyarthritis, polyarthralgia, and/or monoarthritis)
    • Chorea
    • Erythema marginatum
    • Subcutaneous nodule

     

    Supporting Evidence:

    • Importance of clinical history, including:
      • Previous episodes of acute rheumatic fever
      • Presence of streptococcal infection

    Echocardiographic Findings:

    • Recent adaptations include echocardiographic criteria to assess rheumatic heart disease (RHD).
    • Focus on valve abnormalities and functional implications.
    • World Heart Federation (WHF) guidelines provide specific criteria for diagnosing definite and borderline RHD.

Oral iron supplementation at 3-6 mg/kg/day is the first-line treatment for iron deficiency anemia in children. It provides the elemental iron necessary to replenish stores and correct anemia.

 

Iron

Source:

  • Heme sources: meat, poultry, fish.
  • Nonheme sources: dairy, eggs, plant-based foods, breads, cereals, breakfast foods.

 

RDA

  • 1-9 yrs: 7-10 mg/day.
  • Adolescents:11-18 mg/day

 

Iron Deficiency Anemia

Causes:

  • Diminished dietary intake or reduced iron absorption in the proximal small intestine.
  • Excessive loss of body iron.
  • Intercurrent infections (e.g., hookworm infestation, malaria).
  • Dietary inhibitors (e.g., phytates, phosphates, tannates).
  • Cow’s milk is a poor source of bioavailable iron and is not advised for children under 1 year old.

Clinical Features

  • Behavioral: Irritability, anorexia.
  • The pallor of Nail beds, oral mucous membranes, and palpebral conjunctivae are reliable indicators
  • Physical: Weakness, fatigue, leg cramps, breathlessness, tachycardia.
  • Severe cases: Congestive cardiac failure, splenomegaly
  • Severe deficiency signs: Angular stomatitis, glossitis, koilonychia, paronychia

Laboratory Findings:

  • Peripheral blood smear: Microcytic, hypochromic red cells, anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, increased RDW.
  • Reduced MCV and MCHC.
  • Decreased serum iron, increased TIBC, transferrin saturation <16%.
  • Early reduction in serum ferritin, and high free erythroprotoporphyrin (FEP) before anemia.

Treatment

  • Address Underlying Causes: Identify and correct the cause of anemia, such as treating hookworm infestation.
  • Dietary Counseling: Provide guidance on iron-rich foods and avoid inhibitors of iron absorption.
  • Iron Supplementation:
    • Oral iron medications (e.g., ferrous sulfate, 20% elemental iron).
    • Dosage: 3-6 mg/kg/day of elemental iron,
    • Administration: On an empty stomach or between meals for best absorption,
    • Duration: Continue for 4-6 months after anemia correction to replenish iron stores,
    • Monitor reticulocyte count: Should increase within 72-96 hours of therapy initiation,
    • Side effects: Gastrointestinal issues (nausea, discomfort, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea)
  • Parenteral iron therapy: eg Injection Iron sucrose, Injection Ferric carboxymaltose.
  • Blood transfusion: Packed red cell transfusions are essential in emergencies such as severe bleeding, urgent surgery, or severe anemia with congestive heart failure (administered slowly with monitoring).

Iron-rich dietary counseling (Option A) is important but not sufficient as a standalone treatment for established iron deficiency anemia. It should complement iron supplementation.

Intravenous iron administration(Option C) is generally reserved for cases where oral iron is not effective, not tolerated, or when a rapid response is needed, which is not indicated as the initial treatment for this case.

Treatment for intercurrent infections(Option D) should be addressed if an infection is identified as a contributing factor, but the immediate treatment of iron deficiency anemia requires direct iron supplementation.

questions.solution: ng>Rules related to Criminal responsibility: Durham’s rule An accused person is not criminally responsible if his unlawful act is the product of a mental disease or mental defect. Later, this rule was discarded in the USA. Curren’s rule An accused person is not criminally responsible if, at the time of committing the act, he did not have the capacity to regulate his conduct to the requirements of the law as a result of mental disease or defect. McNaughten’s rule (Section 84, IPC, Section 22, BNS ) A person is not criminally responsible if, due to a mental disease, they were unaware of the nature and consequences of their actions or unable to recognise that the act was wrong . It has the following requirements: There must be evidence of a mental disorder. The mental disorder must be present at the time of the crime. The disorder must impair the individual's ability to understand the wrongfulness or illegality of the act. Section 85 IPC (Section 23 BNS) A person who is intoxicated may not be criminally responsible if they were so impaired at the time of the act that they could not understand the nature of their actions or recognize that their actions were wrong or illegal. This applies only if the intoxication was caused against their will or without their knowledge. Section 86 IPC (Section 24 BNS) A voluntarily intoxicated person is still considered criminally responsible if they had the intention or knowledge to commit a crime, despite their intoxication. @Neet_pg_bot

Durham’s rule
  • An accused person is not criminally responsible if his unlawful act is the product of a mental disease or mental defect.
  • Later, this rule was discarded in the USA.

Curren’s rule

An accused person is not criminally responsible if, at the time of committing the act, he did not have the capacity to regulate his conduct to the requirements of the law as a result of mental disease or defect.

McNaughten’s rule

(Section 84, IPC,

Section 22, BNS)
  • A person is not criminally responsible if, due to a mental disease, they were unaware of the nature and consequences of their actions or unable to recognise that the act was wrong.
  • It has the following requirements:
    • There must be evidence of a mental disorder.
    • The mental disorder must be present at the time of the crime.
    • The disorder must impair the individual's ability to understand the wrongfulness or illegality of the act.

Section 85 IPC

(Section 23 BNS)
  • A person who is intoxicated may not be criminally responsible if they were so impaired at the time of the act that they could not understand the nature of their actions or recognize that their actions were wrong or illegal.
  • This applies only if the intoxication was caused against their will or without their knowledge.

Section 86 IPC

(Section 24 BNS)
  • A voluntarily intoxicated person is still considered criminally responsible if they had the intention or knowledge to commit a crime, despite their intoxication.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is the major regulator of carnitine acyltransferase I (CAT-I) activity?
questions.stemHtml: Which one of the following is the major regulator of carnitine acyltransferase I (CAT-I) activity?
questions.solution: Malonyl CoA is the major regulator of CAT-I activity. Malonyl CoA inhibits CAT-I, thus preventing the entry of long-chain acyl groups into the mitochondrial matrix The fate of fatty acid in the cell: Fatty acids (FAs) bind to membrane receptors and enter the cytoplasm via transporters. Fatty acyl CoA synthetase adds CoA to the fatty acids. Carnitine Palmitoyl Transferase 1A (CPT1A) converts fatty acyl CoA to acylcarnitine, which crosses the mitochondrial outer membrane. Inside the matrix, acylcarnitine exchanges with free carnitine through Carnitine Acyl Carnitine Transferase (CACT). Carnitine Palmitoyl Transferase 2 (CPT2) then converts acylcarnitine back to acyl-CoA esters. Regulation By CAT-I: Mobilized fatty acids enter mitochondria for beta-oxidation. Carnitine acyl transferase I (CAT-I) regulates this entry. In Low energy states: Conditions like diabetes and starvation, Glucagon levels increase. Increased glucagon decreases malonyl CoA levels. Reduced malonyl CoA levels lead to increased beta-oxidation in the mitochondria. In High energy states: Insulin levels are high. Increased insulin increases malonyl CoA levels. Increased malonyl CoA leads to decreased fatty acid oxidation Hence, Acyl CoA gets stored in the form of TAG in the cells Insulin and glucagon (Option A and B) do not directly influence CAT-1 but their levels indirectly influence it, by increasing or decreasing malonyl COA levels. ATP (Option D) does not directly regulate CAT-I activity. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Malonyl CoA is the major regulator of CAT-I activity. Malonyl CoA inhibits CAT-I, thus preventing the entry of long-chain acyl groups into the mitochondrial matrix

 

The fate of fatty acid in the cell:

 

  • Fatty acids (FAs) bind to membrane receptors and enter the cytoplasm via transporters.
  • Fatty acyl CoA synthetase adds CoA to the fatty acids.
  • Carnitine Palmitoyl Transferase 1A (CPT1A) converts fatty acyl CoA to acylcarnitine, which crosses the mitochondrial outer membrane.
  • Inside the matrix, acylcarnitine exchanges with free carnitine through Carnitine Acyl Carnitine Transferase (CACT).
  • Carnitine Palmitoyl Transferase 2 (CPT2) then converts acylcarnitine back to acyl-CoA esters.

Regulation By CAT-I:

  • Mobilized fatty acids enter mitochondria for beta-oxidation.
  • Carnitine acyl transferase I (CAT-I) regulates this entry.
  • In Low energy states:
    • Conditions like diabetes and starvation,
    • Glucagon levels increase.
    • Increased glucagon decreases malonyl CoA levels.
    • Reduced malonyl CoA levels lead to increased beta-oxidation in the mitochondria.
  • In High energy states:
    • Insulin levels are high.
    • Increased insulin increases malonyl CoA levels.
    • Increased malonyl CoA leads to decreased fatty acid oxidation
    • Hence, Acyl CoA gets stored in the form of TAG in the cells

Insulin and glucagon (Option A and B) do not directly influence CAT-1 but their levels indirectly influence it, by increasing or decreasing malonyl COA levels.
 

ATP (Option D) does not directly regulate CAT-I activity.

The Ujjawala scheme

The Ujjawala scheme, launched in India on December 4, 2007, by the Ministry of Women and Child Development, is a comprehensive program to combat trafficking. The scheme is primarily implemented through NGOs.

Objectives/Goals

Strategies to Achieve Goals

Prevention

  • Formation of community vigilance and adolescent groups, awareness creation
  • preparation of IEC (Information, Education, Communication) material, organization of workshops.

Rescue

  • Safe withdrawal of victims from the place of exploitation.

Rehabilitation

  • Providing safe shelter, basic amenities, medical care, legal aid, vocational training, and employment opportunities to victims.

Reintegration

  • Supporting victims in their reintegration into society.

Repatriation

  • Providing support to cross-border victims for their safe return to their home countries.

 

The Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY) (Option B) is a key initiative to provide rural and underprivileged households with access to clean cooking fuels like LPG, replacing traditional cooking fuels. It comes under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas (MOPNG)

The PM Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana (PM Saubhagya scheme) (Option D) was initiated in September 2017 to provide electricity to every household by December 2018. The Ministry of Power administers it.

questions.solution: epam is the drug of choice for the management of status epilepticus due to its rapid onset of action and effectiveness in terminating seizures. It acts by enhancing the effects of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) in the brain, thereby reducing neuronal excitability and terminating seizures. Management of status epilepticus: Position the head, provide oxygen, and monitor vital signs. ↓ Establish vascular access and check glucose levels. ↓ Administer benzodiazepines (preferably lorazepam IV). ↓ If seizures persist after 2 doses of benzodiazepines. ↓ Administer antiepileptic drugs (Fosphenytoin, Phenytoin, Levetiracetam, Valproic acid). ↓ If refractory status epilepticus suspected ↓ Initiate continuous infusion of Midazolam, Pentobarbital, Thiopental, or Propofol. Phenobarbital (Option A) and Valproate (Option D) are used in the management of status epilepticus but are not the first-line treatments. Intravenous administration of Lamotrigine (Option C) is contraindicated in emergency situations due to its association with Stevens-Johnson syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: ation: Ammonium chloride is used to promote urinary drug excretion in cases of Amphetamine poisoning Amphetamine Poisoning: Abused as “ performance-enhancing drugs ” among students and sportspersons. Also called “ rave party drugs ”: Ecstasy/crystal/ methamphetamine/MDMA. Triad : Sudden psychosis + Hypertension + Golden coloured urine. Treatment: Ammonium chloride turns the urine pH acidic and causes forced diuresis of basic drugs like amphetamines. Chlorpromazine : treats psychosis and hypertension through alpha-blocking action. Intravenous sodium bicarbonate (Option A): is used for urinary alkalization in cases of salicylate poisoning (weak acid), which manifests as tinnitus, nausea, and vomiting. Flumazenil (Option B): is used to reverse the effects of benzodiazepine poisoning, which appears with symptoms of CNS depression and impaired mental status. der-top:1px solid #000000; vertical-align:top">

Hypocalcemia

Due to decreased calcium absorption in the intestine.

Hypophosphatemia

Due to decreased phosphate absorption in the intestine and decreased reabsorption of phosphate in the kidneys.

Secondary Hyperparathyroidism

In response to low calcium levels, the parathyroid hormone (PTH) increases, which increases calcium reabsorption from bone and the kidneys.

Elevated Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)

Due to Increased bone turnover as a result of increased PTH.

25-hydroxy cholecalciferol

Decreased.

 

Prolonged secondary hyperparathyroidism can cause renal osteodystrophy, which may lead to pathological fractures.

Primary hyperparathyroidism (Option B) leads to excess PTH production, causing hypercalcemia.

Hypoparathyroidism (Option C) presents with low PTH and hypocalcemia. Hypothyroidism is commonly associated with vitamin D deficiency, potentially due to immune dysfunction and impacts on calcium metabolism

Chronic kidney disease (Option D) causes secondary hyperparathyroidism due to impaired phosphate excretion and low 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D levels, it is typically associated with hyperphosphatemia.

questions.stem: What is the major concern associated with bupivacaine toxicity?
questions.stemHtml: What is the major concern associated with bupivacaine toxicity?
questions.solution: tid="6bfc8ecaa9169277718345b55b3bd5">cardiotoxic effects, particularly when administered in high doses or if accidentally injected into a blood vessel, which can lead to severe cardiac arrhythmias and cardiac arrest. Bupivacaine Classification Bupivacaine is an amide-type local anesthetic Mechanism of Action It works by blocking sodium channels in nerve membranes, preventing the propagation of nerve impulses, which results in local anesthesia. Clinical Uses Commonly used for spinal, epidural, and peripheral nerve blocks. Widely used in labor and delivery for epidural anesthesia and in long-duration surgeries. Duration of Action Longer duration of action compared to other local anesthetics like lidocaine. It can provide anesthesia for several hours, making it ideal for prolonged procedures. Onset of Action Has a slower onset (10-15 minutes) compared to faster-acting anesthetics like lidocaine. Cardiotoxicity Major concern with bupivacaine is its potential for cardiotoxicity, especially at higher doses or when inadvertently injected intravenously, leading to severe arrhythmias or cardiac arrest. Metabolism Metabolized primarily in the liver by cytochrome P450 enzymes and excreted by the kidneys. Enantiomers The S-enantiomer of bupivacaine, known as levobupivacaine, is associated with reduced cardiotoxicity and is often used as a safer alternative. Lipid Solubility & Protein Binding Bupivacaine has high lipid solubility and high protein binding, which contributes to its prolonged duration of action. Contraindications Should be avoided in patients with severe cardiac arrhythmias, and caution should be used in patients with liver disease due to its hepatic metabolism. Common Side Effects In addition to cardiotoxicity, other potential side effects include CNS toxicity, such as dizziness, seizures, and lightheadedness, especially with accidental intravascular injection. Toxicity Direct intravenous injection or rapid vascular uptake of the drug is the most common reason for bupivacaine toxicity, which has an upper limit of 2.5 to 3.5 mg/kg upper limit of dosing. Treatment for toxicity: 20% intralipid solution. @Neet_pg_bot

tid="6bfc8ecaa9169277718345b55b3bd5">cardiotoxic effects, particularly when administered in high doses or if accidentally injected into a blood vessel, which can lead to severe cardiac arrhythmias and cardiac arrest.

 

Bupivacaine

Classification
  • Bupivacaine is an amide-type local anesthetic

Mechanism of Action

  • It works by blocking sodium channels in nerve membranes, preventing the propagation of nerve impulses, which results in local anesthesia.

Clinical Uses

  • Commonly used for spinal, epidural, and peripheral nerve blocks.
  • Widely used in labor and delivery for epidural anesthesia and in long-duration surgeries.

Duration of Action
  • Longer duration of action compared to other local anesthetics like lidocaine. It can provide anesthesia for several hours, making it ideal for prolonged procedures.

Onset of Action
  • Has a slower onset (10-15 minutes) compared to faster-acting anesthetics like lidocaine.

Cardiotoxicity
  • Major concern with bupivacaine is its potential for cardiotoxicity, especially at higher doses or when inadvertently injected intravenously, leading to severe arrhythmias or cardiac arrest.

Metabolism
  • Metabolized primarily in the liver by cytochrome P450 enzymes and excreted by the kidneys.

Enantiomers
  • The S-enantiomer of bupivacaine, known as levobupivacaine, is associated with reduced cardiotoxicity and is often used as a safer alternative.

Lipid Solubility & Protein Binding

  • Bupivacaine has high lipid solubility and high protein binding, which contributes to its prolonged duration of action.

Contraindications
  • Should be avoided in patients with severe cardiac arrhythmias, and caution should be used in patients with liver disease due to its hepatic metabolism.

Common Side Effects
  • In addition to cardiotoxicity, other potential side effects include CNS toxicity, such as dizziness, seizures, and lightheadedness, especially with accidental intravascular injection.

Toxicity
  • Direct intravenous injection or rapid vascular uptake of the drug is the most common reason for bupivacaine toxicity, which has an upper limit of 2.5 to 3.5 mg/kg upper limit of dosing.
  • Treatment for toxicity: 20% intralipid solution.

questions.stem: In the Complement Fixation Test (CFT), what indicates a positive result?
questions.stemHtml: In the Complement Fixation Test (CFT), what indicates a positive result?

options.label: A
options.text: Lysis of sheep red blood cells

options.label: B
options.text: Formation of an immune complex between antigen and antibody

options.label: C
options.text: No lysis of sheep red blood cells

options.label: D
options.text: Presence of active complement in the serum

questions.answerText: No lysis of sheep red blood cells
questions.solution: lement Fixation Test (CFT): Purpose : Detects specific antigens or antibodies in serum by measuring complement fixation. Principle : Immune complex (antigen-antibody binding) fixes complement, which is then detected using sensitised sheep red blood cells. Example : Wassermann reaction for syphilis diagnosis. No lysis of sheep red blood cells indicates a positive CFT. Procedure of CFT: Step Description Step 1: Complement Fixation 1. Heat patient serum to inactivate native complement. 2. Add known antigen or antibody and complement. 3. Immune complex fixes the complement if a specific antigen or antibody is present. Step 2: Indicator Stage 1. Add sensitised SRBCs (coated with amboceptor) to the mixture. 2. Positive CFT: Complement fixed, no SRBC lysis. 3. Negative CFT: Free complement lyses SRBCs. Indirect Complement Fixation Test: Modification : Used for sera that cannot fix guinea pig complement (e.g., avian/mammalian sera). Method : Add standard antiserum that can fix complement after the first CFT stage. Positive Result : Hemolysis occurs if antigen-antibody binding has consumed the complement. Other Complement-Dependent Serological Tests: Immune adherence : Bacteria stick to cells via antibodies + complement Immobilisation : Antibodies + complement inhibit bacterial motility Cytolytic/cytocidal : Antibodies + complement lyse/kill bacteria Lysis of sheep red blood cells (Option A) indicates a negative result, as it shows that the complement was not fixed, and the sheep RBCs are free to be lysed. Formation of an immune complex (Option B) occurs in both positive and negative results but does not directly indicate a positive outcome. Presence of active complement in the serum (Option C) before heating could interfere with the test, but it is not an indicator of a positive result. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
lement Fixation Test (CFT):
  • Purpose: Detects specific antigens or antibodies in serum by measuring complement fixation.
  • Principle: Immune complex (antigen-antibody binding) fixes complement, which is then detected using sensitised sheep red blood cells.
  • Example: Wassermann reaction for syphilis diagnosis.
  • No lysis of sheep red blood cells indicates a positive CFT.

Procedure of CFT:

Step

Description

Step 1: Complement Fixation

1. Heat patient serum to inactivate native complement.

2. Add known antigen or antibody and complement.

3. Immune complex fixes the complement if a specific antigen or antibody is present.

Step 2: Indicator Stage

1. Add sensitised SRBCs (coated with amboceptor) to the mixture.

2. Positive CFT: Complement fixed, no SRBC lysis.

3. Negative CFT: Free complement lyses SRBCs.

Indirect Complement Fixation Test:

  • Modification: Used for sera that cannot fix guinea pig complement (e.g., avian/mammalian sera).
  • Method: Add standard antiserum that can fix complement after the first CFT stage.
    • Positive Result: Hemolysis occurs if antigen-antibody binding has consumed the complement.

Other Complement-Dependent Serological Tests:

  • Immune adherence: Bacteria stick to cells via antibodies + complement

  • Immobilisation: Antibodies + complement inhibit bacterial motility

  • Cytolytic/cytocidal: Antibodies + complement lyse/kill bacteria

 

Lysis of sheep red blood cells (Option A) indicates a negative result, as it shows that the complement was not fixed, and the sheep RBCs are free to be lysed.

Formation of an immune complex (Option B) occurs in both positive and negative results but does not directly indicate a positive outcome.

Presence of active complement in the serum (Option C) before heating could interfere with the test, but it is not an indicator of a positive result.
