strong>Clonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that helps reduce the autonomic symptoms of opioid withdrawal, such as sweating, restlessness, tachycardia, and hypertension.
  • It works by decreasing sympathetic outflow, which alleviates symptoms like piloerection, tremors, and rhinorrhea.
  • Clonidine is particularly useful in patients who are unwilling to use opioid-based treatments as in this patient.
  • Methadone (Option A) and Buprenorphine and Naloxone combination therapy (Options B & D) are opioid agonists used for maintenance therapy, but this patient prefers a non-opioid treatment.

 

Opioid withdrawal symptoms include

  • Muscle and Bone aches, Abdominal cramps
  • Diarrhea, Lacrimation, Rhinorrhea, Sweating - resembles flu
  • Piloerection/ Gooseflesh ("Cold Turkey" Means Abstinence Syndrome)
  • Frequent yawning, Insomnia
  • Mydriasis
  • Hypertension, Tachycardia
  • Temperature Dysregulation (Hypothermia Or Hyperthermia)
  • Nausea, vomiting, and restlessness

 

Treatment of Opioid Withdrawal

Detoxification

Maintenance
  • Opioid Agents
  • Methadone: Opioid Agonist.
  • Buprenorphine:Partial Opioid Agonist.

Opioid Substitution Therapy (OST):

  • Methadone: Full opioid agonist
    • Improves treatment retention and reduces criminal behavior.
    • 80–120 mg/day.
    • Side effects: constipation, sweating, sexual dysfunction.
  • Buprenorphine:
    • Partial opioid agonist with a ceiling effect (limits overdose risk).
    • Combined with naloxone to prevent abuse.
    • Taken sublingually (tablet/film).
    • Side effects: constipation, nausea, drowsiness.
 
  • Opioid Antagonists (Naloxone, Naltrexone):
    • Naloxone: Reverses opioid overdose (emergency use).
    • Naltrexone: Blocks opioid effects to prevent euphoria, reduces opioid cravings. Available in oral and long-acting injectable forms.
    • Does not cause dependence or withdrawal but requires patient adherence.

Opioid addicted patient but unwilling to be treated with opioids: Symptomatic agents

  • Clonidine
    • Alpha-2 Adrenergic Agonist.
    • Reduces autonomic withdrawal symptoms- Sweating, Restlessness, Tremor or Rhinorrhea.
  • Anxiety: Benzodiazepines
  • Insomnia: Zolpidem
  • Musculoskeletal Pain: NSAIDs (Ibuprofen)
  • GI Symptoms: Antiemetic Diarrhea (Loperamide)

Pregnant Women with Opioid Use Disorder:

  • Illicit opioid use during pregnancy increases risks for both mother and baby
  • Methadone or buprenorphine maintenance reduces risks, though neonatal opioid withdrawal may still occur.
  • Associated risks- Neonatal infections (HIV), premature labor, low birth weight, and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

Psychotherapy Modalities/ Non- Pharmacological Treatment:

  • Effective treatments: Individual therapy, CBT, family therapy, support groups (NA), and social skills training.
  • Social skills training is key for patients with poor social skills.
  • Residential programs for people with substance use disorders.
  • Education on HIV transmission and safe sex is essential.
  • Needle-exchange programs, where available, help reduce unsafe needle sharing and associated infections.
  • Narcotics Anonymous (NA): A 12-step self-help group for abstinent drug addicts.

 

Naloxone (Option D) is a short-acting opioid antagonist used for reversing opioid overdose, not for treating withdrawal.

questions.stem: Based on the graph showing potassium ion permeability during an action potential, at which point does the permeability of potassium ions reach its peak?
questions.stemHtml: Based on the graph showing potassium ion permeability during an action potential, at which point does the permeability of potassium ions reach its peak?
questions.solution: Point D signifies the early phase of repolarization. At this stage, voltage-gated potassium channels are fully open, leading to the highest permeability to potassium ions. Resting Membrane Potential ( Point A on graph): At rest, the neuron's membrane potential is around -70 mV. K+ permeability is higher than Na+ permeability due to the presence of K+ leak channels. However, the overall permeability to both ions is relatively low. Depolarization Phase (Between Points A and C): Voltage-gated Na+ channels open faster than K+ channels. Rapid influx of Na+ ions, causing a rapid rise in membrane potential, causing a steep slope. Peak of Action Potential (Point C) : Na+ permeability is at its maximum. K+ channels are also opening at this stage but have not reached their peak. Early Repolarization Phase (Point D) : Early phase of repolarization. questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman presents with lower abdominal discomfort. Ultrasound reveals a 5 cm unilocular cystic mass adjacent to the left ovary but separate from it. The ovary itself appears normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: s are cystic structures in the broad ligament adjacent to but separate from the ovary. Origin: Typically non-neoplastic; arise from paramesonephric duct remnants or mesothelial inclusion cysts. Ultrasound appearance: Unilocular, thin-walled cysts. Symptoms: Often asymptomatic; discovered incidentally during imaging or surgery. Mimicry: When symptomatic, can mimic ovarian cysts. Imaging limitations: Difficult to distinguish from ovarian pathology; managed like ovarian cysts. Treatment: Usually cystectomy or drainage with fulguration. Solid tumors: Rare; most commonly leiomyomas. Management of solid tumors: Typically removed due to the inability to rule out malignancy via imaging alone. Theca lutein cysts (Option A) are usually bilateral and multiple, originate from the ovary itself, and are associated with ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome or gestational trophoblastic disease. Functional ovarian cysts (Option B) originate from the ovary and typically present with a normal-appearing ovary. They are typically smaller (usually < 3 cm), except for a large corpus luteum cyst. Ovarian fibroma (Option D) is a solid tumor of the ovary, appearing as a solid mass within the ovary rather than a cystic structure, and is typically seen in older women (perimenopausal or postmenopausal). @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
s are cystic structures in the broad ligament adjacent to but separate from the ovary.

  • Origin: Typically non-neoplastic; arise from paramesonephric duct remnants or mesothelial inclusion cysts.

  • Ultrasound appearance: Unilocular, thin-walled cysts.

  • Symptoms: Often asymptomatic; discovered incidentally during imaging or surgery.

  • Mimicry: When symptomatic, can mimic ovarian cysts.

  • Imaging limitations: Difficult to distinguish from ovarian pathology; managed like ovarian cysts.

  • Treatment: Usually cystectomy or drainage with fulguration.

  • Solid tumors: Rare; most commonly leiomyomas.

  • Management of solid tumors: Typically removed due to the inability to rule out malignancy via imaging alone.

 

Theca lutein cysts (Option A) are usually bilateral and multiple, originate from the ovary itself, and are associated with ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome or gestational trophoblastic disease.

 

Functional ovarian cysts (Option B) originate from the ovary and typically present with a normal-appearing ovary. They are typically smaller (usually < 3 cm), except for a large corpus luteum cyst.

 

Ovarian fibroma (Option D) is a solid tumor of the ovary, appearing as a solid mass within the ovary rather than a cystic structure, and is typically seen in older women (perimenopausal or postmenopausal).

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the most accurate statement regarding the role of ultrasonography (USG) and laparoscopy in the diagnosis of genital tuberculosis (TB) in women?

options.label: A
options.text: USG can definitively diagnose genital TB by detecting specific tuberculous lesions in the pelvic organs.

options.label: B
options.text: Laparoscopy is mainly used to assess the extent of tubal damage in genital TB, and it allows for direct visualization and biopsy of the affected tissues.

options.label: C
options.text: USG is more effective than laparoscopy in identifying tubal obstruction caused by genital TB.

options.label: D
options.text: Both USG and laparoscopy are equally effective in diagnosing genital TB and can be used interchangeably.

questions.answerText: Laparoscopy is mainly used to assess the extent of tubal damage in genital TB, and it allows for direct visualization and biopsy of the affected tissues.
questions.solution: biopsy of the affected tissues. Explanation: Laparoscopy is a crucial tool for diagnosing genital TB because it permits direct visualization of the pelvic organs, identification of lesions, and allows for biopsy collection and fluid aspiration for culture, which is essential for a definitive diagnosis. USG, while useful for identifying abnormalities and guiding further investigation, cannot definitively diagnose genital TB or assess tubal damage as accurately as laparoscopy can (also assess feasibility of adhiolysis in severe distortion). Investigations for Pelvic Tuberculosis: Blood: Total leucocyte count and ESR may be raised Mantoux test: less specific Chest X-ray: To look for evidence of healed or active pulmonary lesions Diagnostic uterine curettage One part in normal-saline for: Histopathological examination to detect the giant cell system. One part in normal saline for: Culture in Löwenstein-Jensen media Identification of the acid-fast bacilli by Ziehl- Neelsen’s stain (AFB-microscopy) Nucleic acid amplification Guinea pig inoculation. Liquid culture Nucleic acid amplification test GeneXpert (CBNAAT) Biopsy Hysterosalpingography (HSG): In a proven case, HSG is contraindicated for the risk of reactivation of the lesion. Imaging: USG, IVU, CT, MRI Laparoscopy Hysteroscopy @Neet_pg_bot

biopsy of the affected tissues.

Explanation:

Laparoscopy is a crucial tool for diagnosing genital TB because it permits direct visualization of the pelvic organs, identification of lesions, and allows for biopsy collection and fluid aspiration for culture, which is essential for a definitive diagnosis.

USG, while useful for identifying abnormalities and guiding further investigation, cannot definitively diagnose genital TB or assess tubal damage as accurately as laparoscopy can (also assess feasibility of adhiolysis in severe distortion).

Investigations for Pelvic Tuberculosis:

  • Blood: Total leucocyte count and ESR may be raised
  • Mantoux test: less specific
  • Chest X-ray: To look for evidence of healed or active pulmonary lesions
  • Diagnostic uterine curettage
    • One part in normal-saline for:
      • Histopathological examination to detect the giant cell system.
    • One part in normal saline for:
      • Culture in Löwenstein-Jensen media
      • Identification of the acid-fast bacilli by Ziehl- Neelsen’s stain (AFB-microscopy)
      • Nucleic acid amplification
      • Guinea pig inoculation.
    • Liquid culture
    • Nucleic acid amplification test
    • GeneXpert (CBNAAT)
  • Biopsy
  • Hysterosalpingography (HSG): In a proven case, HSG is contraindicated for the risk of reactivation of the lesion.
  • Imaging: USG, IVU, CT, MRI
  • Laparoscopy
  • Hysteroscopy

  • The lesion appears as a white, corrugated (or hairy) patch that cannot be wiped off, which matches the presentation in the image.

    • Disease associated with EBV

    Pathognomonic Findings

    Classic Symptoms

    Infectious Mononucleosis

    Atypical lymphocytosis, positive heterophile antibody test, elevated liver enzymes
    • Fever
    • Pharyngitis, Lymphadenopathy (posterior cervical)
    • Splenomegaly

    Burkitt Lymphoma

    "Starry sky" appearance on histology
    • Rapidly growing jaw or abdominal mass

    Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma

    Undifferentiated carcinoma with EBV DNA in tumor cells
    • Nasal obstruction
    • Epistaxis
    • Hearing loss
    • Cervical lymphadenopathy

    Hodgkin Lymphoma

    Reed-Sternberg cells on histology
    • Painless lymphadenopathy
    • B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), pruritus

    Oral Hairy Leukoplakia

    White, hairy patches on lateral tongue, non-scrapable
    • Asymptomatic, common in immunocompromised individuals

    EBV-associated Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)

    Hemophagocytosis in bone marrow/tissues
    • Fever
    • Hepatosplenomegaly
    • Cytopenias
    • Hyperferritinemia
    • Hypertriglyceridemia

    Gastric Carcinoma

    EBV DNA in gastric carcinoma
    • Weight loss
    • Abdominal pain
    • Nausea and Vomiting

    Candida (Option A): It typically causes oral thrush, which presents as white plaques that can be wiped off, unlike the corrugated lesion shown in the image.

    • Erythematous Candidiasis

    Human Herpes Virus (HHV6) (Option C): It is not commonly associated with oral lesions in immunocompromised patients. HHV-6 more often reactivates to cause roseola in infants or is asymptomatic in adults.

Causes of Isolated Abortion

Causes of Recurrent Abortion

Chromosomal abnormalities are the most common causes of early miscarriages.

  • Thyroid abnormalities
  • Diabetes mellitus
 

Cervicouterine factors:

  • Intrauterine adhesions
  • Cervical incompetence
  • Mullerian anomalies
 

Environmental factors:

  • Smoking and alcohol consumption
  • Contraceptive agents like IUD

Parental Chromosomal Abnormalities.

  • Robertsonian translocations
  • Inversions
  • Aneuploidies
  • Other structural chromosomal abnormalities
 

Anatomical Factors:

  • Asherman Syndrome
  • Uterine Polyps
  • Mullerian Defects, most commonly septate uterus
 

Immunological Factors:

  • SLE
  • APLA
 

Endocrine Factors:

  • Overt Hypothyroidism and Iodine Deficiency
  • Subclinical Hypothyroidism with Anti-Thyroid Antibodies

questions.stem: Which of the following contraceptive agents are used as the first-line agents in heavy menstrual bleeding?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following contraceptive agents are used as the first-line agents in heavy menstrual bleeding?
questions.solution: ng>Combined Oral Contraceptives (POPs), thin the endometrial lining, preventing its build-up. This results in lighter menstrual periods and is an effective mechanism for reducing heavy menstrual bleeding. Hence, it is the first-line agent used in heavy menstrual bleeding. Progesterone is prescribed to control abnormal bleeding, as it has fewer withdrawal effects and stabilises the endometrium. If progesterone is ineffective, estrogen is given to prevent excessive bleeding. Progesterone-only pills (Option B) are used in the treatment of heavy bleeding & dysmenorrhea. It is the drug of choice for lactating women. Copper-containing Intrauterine Device (IUD) (Option C) are contraindicated in heavy menstrual bleeding as they are known to cause heavy menstrual bleeding. Contraceptive patch (Option D) can also be effective in managing menstrual bleeding, but progesterone-only pills are used as the first-line agents. @Neet_pg_bot

048f04ce29">cortical defects show a cold spot

 

Bone scan:

 

Definition

Nuclear medicine study using technetium-99m (Tc-99m-MDP)

Absorption

~50% of injected dose absorbed by bones (2-6 hours post-injection)

Phases of Study

1. Immediate phase

2. Blood pool phase

3. Delayed phase

4. Optional delayed phase

Indications
  • Detection and follow-up of skeletal metastases
  • Radiographically occult fractures (e.g., stress fractures)
  • Osteomyelitis
  • Complex regional pain syndrome
  • Evaluation of hip joint prosthesis for infection or loosening
  • Paget disease

Patient Preparation
  • Optimal hydration
  • Remove metal objects
  • Void before study

Conditions Affecting Uptake
  • Increased uptake in kidneys/liver in conditions like thalassemia and hemochromatosis
  • Poor image quality with reduced renal function

Tracer Dose
  • 740 - 925 Mbq (20 - 25 mCi) administered intravenously in adults

Renal Uptake
  • Useful for detecting renal abnormalities; faint/absent uptake commonly due to renal insufficiency

Results

Normal: If the radiotracer is present evenly throughout all the bones.

Abnormal:

  • Will show hot spots or cold spots as compared to surrounding bone.
  • Hot spots are areas where there is an increased collection of radioactive material.
  • Cold spots are areas that have taken up less of the radioactive material.

Hot Spots

Areas of new bone formation; are seen in:

  • Fractures
  • Osteomyelitis
  • Osteoblastic bone metastasis

Cold Spots

Seen in:

  • Multiple myeloma (normal alkaline phosphatase)
  • Fibrous cortical defects (VS fibrous dysplasia shows hot spots)

Physiological Presence
  • Tracer present in the bladder due to renal excretion (Option B)

Superscan:

  • Multiple bones show hot spots without kidney uptake.
  • Seen in conditions that affect multiple bones, like hyperparathyroidism and renal failure. (Option D)

Triple-Phase Bone Scan:

 

Criteria

Delayed Phase Imaging

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a cause of lacrimal pump failure, leading to excessive tearing (epiphora)?
questions.solution: lies on the proper function of the orbicularis oculi muscle and the correct positioning of the punctum. In Bell’s palsy, weakness of the orbicularis oculi muscle prevents proper eyelid closure and tear drainage, as the orbicularis oculi muscle is involved in both the tear suction and drainage phase of the lacrimal pump mechanism. This leads to epiphora (excessive tearing). Trauma to the canaliculus (Option A): While an injury to the canaliculus can block the tear drainage system, it does not directly disrupt the lacrimal pump mechanism. Obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct (Option C): This condition involves a blockage in the nasolacrimal duct, preventing proper tear drainage. Narrowing of the punctum (Option D): Punctal stenosis refers to a narrowing or closure of the punctum (the opening at the corner of the eyelid that drains tears). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Before performing radial artery cannulation on a 7-year-old child for continuous blood pressure monitoring during major surgery, the anesthesiologist compresses both the radial and ulnar arteries, asks the child to make a fist, then releases the ulnar artery while keeping the radial artery compressed. What is the primary purpose of this maneuver?
questions.stemHtml: Before performing radial artery cannulation on a 7-year-old child for continuous blood pressure monitoring during major surgery, the anesthesiologist compresses both the radial and ulnar arteries, asks the child to make a fist, then releases the ulnar artery while keeping the radial artery compressed. What is the primary purpose of this maneuver?

options.label: A
options.text: To assess the elasticity of the arterial walls

options.label: B
options.text: To evaluate collateral circulation in the hand

options.label: C
options.text: To determine the size of the radial artery

questions.answerText: To evaluate collateral circulation in the hand
questions.solution: on: This maneuver, known as the Modified Allen's test , is a non-invasive procedure used primarily to evaluate the collateral circulation in the hand before radial artery cannulation. Its main purposes are: To assess the patency and adequacy of the ulnar artery To evaluate the completeness of the palmar arch The test is performed as follows: Both ulnar and radial arteries are compressed. The child is asked to clench their fist several times to expel blood from the hand. The hand is then opened, appearing pale. Pressure on the ulnar artery is released while maintaining compression on the radial artery. If the hand flushes within 5-7 seconds, it indicates adequate collateral circulation through the ulnar artery. A positive test (rapid flushing) suggests that it's safe to proceed with radial artery catheterization , as the ulnar artery can adequately perfuse the hand if the radial artery is compromised during or after the procedure. A negative test , where the hand fails to flush within 5-15 seconds, suggests inadequate or absent ulnar circulation . In this case, avoid puncturing the radial artery, as it is the sole source of arterial blood to that hand. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
on:
  • This maneuver, known as the Modified Allen's test, is a non-invasive procedure used primarily to evaluate the collateral circulation in the hand before radial artery cannulation. Its main purposes are:
    • To assess the patency and adequacy of the ulnar artery
    • To evaluate the completeness of the palmar arch
  • The test is performed as follows:
    • Both ulnar and radial arteries are compressed.
    • The child is asked to clench their fist several times to expel blood from the hand.
    • The hand is then opened, appearing pale.
    • Pressure on the ulnar artery is released while maintaining compression on the radial artery.
    • If the hand flushes within 5-7 seconds, it indicates adequate collateral circulation through the ulnar artery.

  • A positive test (rapid flushing) suggests that it's safe to proceed with radial artery catheterization, as the ulnar artery can adequately perfuse the hand if the radial artery is compromised during or after the procedure.
  • A negative test, where the hand fails to flush within 5-15 seconds, suggests inadequate or absent ulnar circulation.
  • In this case, avoid puncturing the radial artery, as it is the sole source of arterial blood to that hand.

questions.stem: A 26 y/o male from a rural area in India presents to the clinic with complaints of anxiety, fatigue, and weakness. He is preoccupied with the belief that he is losing semen during urination and nocturnal emissions. He also describes his semen as "milk-like." He is concerned that this will lead to physical weakness and impotence. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 26 y/o male from a rural area in India presents to the clinic with complaints of anxiety, fatigue, and weakness. He is preoccupied with the belief that he is losing semen during urination and nocturnal emissions. He also describes his semen as "milk-like." He is concerned that this will lead to physical weakness and impotence. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.solution: >Dhat syndrome is characterized by the fear of semen loss through nocturnal emission, urination, or other means, leading to anxiety, somatic complaints, and weakness, which fits the patient's presentation. His cultural background and the description of his semen as "milk-like" align with the typical presentation of Dhat syndrome. Culture bound syndromes: patterned behaviors of distress or illness whose symptoms appear distinct from psychiatric categories and considered unique to particular cultural settings. Such as Dhat syndrome and Koro syndrome. Dhat syndrome Koro syndrome Definition : A psychiatric condition marked by fear of semen loss through ejaculation, nocturnal emission, or other means. Cultural Context : Leading culture-bound syndrome in the Indian subcontinent, tied to Ayurvedic beliefs that semen is vital for health. Demographics : Affects young, unmarried males from lower socioeconomic and rural backgrounds. Age : The average onset is around 26 years. This can lead to depression and sexual dysfunction Clinical Presentation Symptoms : Anxiety, fatigue, weakness, and impotence from the fear of semen loss. Beliefs : Semen loss through nocturnal emissions, urination, defecation, or arousal. Somatic Complaints : Physical symptoms tied to weakness, infertility, and fear of death. Semen Description : Often described as "milk-like" or "pus-like." Treatment Psychiatric Care : Treated similarly to depression, with psychotherapy (sex education to dispel the myths) and antidepressants. Diagnosis ICD-10 : Concern over semen loss (seen as whitish discharge in urine) with associated anxiety and physical symptoms. Female Dhat syndrome , presenting with nonpathological vaginal discharge ("safedpaani") seen as a vital fluid, is triggered by warm foods, stress, and dietary imbalances, causing somatic symptoms and linked to Ayurvedic beliefs about bodily balance. Definition : A psychiatric disorder characterized by an intense fear of genital retraction into the body, believed to result in death (in males, the penis; in females, the vulva or breasts). Epidemiology : Epidemic Koro : Common in parts of East and Southeast Asia (e.g., China, India, Malaysia), linked to cultural beliefs and myths. Sporadic Koro : Occurs globally, unrelated to culture, often secondary to psychiatric disorders (e.g., schizophrenia, depression) or substance use. Clinical Presentation : Overwhelming anxiety with belief of genital retraction and impending death. Symptoms: Panic attacks, physical attempts to prevent retraction, measuring genitals, insomnia, and fear of death Treatment : Psychotherapy : Sex education and counselling to dispel myths. Medications : Anxiolytics, antidepressants, antipsychotics, and sedatives (based on psychiatric comorbidities). Koro syndrome (Option A) involves the fear of genital retraction rather than semen loss and is prevalent in different regions of Asia. Premature ejaculation (Option C) is a sexual dysfunction, but the focus in this case is on semen loss and its perceived effects, not on ejaculation timing. Hypochondriasis (Option D) involves excessive health anxiety, but Dhat syndrome specifically involves culturally bound fears of semen loss rather than general health anxiety. @Neet_pg_bot

      • Epidemic Koro: Common in parts of East and Southeast Asia (e.g., China, India, Malaysia), linked to cultural beliefs and myths.
      • Sporadic Koro: Occurs globally, unrelated to culture, often secondary to psychiatric disorders (e.g., schizophrenia, depression) or substance use.
    • Clinical Presentation:
      • Overwhelming anxiety with belief of genital retraction and impending death.
      • Symptoms: Panic attacks, physical attempts to prevent retraction, measuring genitals, insomnia, and fear of death
    • Treatment:
      • Psychotherapy: Sex education and counselling to dispel myths.
      • Medications: Anxiolytics, antidepressants, antipsychotics, and sedatives (based on psychiatric comorbidities).


     

    Koro syndrome (Option A) involves the fear of genital retraction rather than semen loss and is prevalent in different regions of Asia.

    Premature ejaculation (Option C) is a sexual dysfunction, but the focus in this case is on semen loss and its perceived effects, not on ejaculation timing.

    Hypochondriasis (Option D) involves excessive health anxiety, but Dhat syndrome specifically involves culturally bound fears of semen loss rather than general health anxiety.

questions.solution: The clinical presentation of a 10-year-old child with palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, elevated serum IgA levels, and RBC casts in urine is suggestive of Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP). Clinical features (PAAARpura): P: Palpable purpura (typically lower extremities and buttocks) A: Arthralgia / joint pain A: Abdominal involvement (pain, nausea, GI bleeding possible) A: Associated with elevated IgA (causative immunoglobulin) R: Renal involvement (hematuria, red blood cell casts) Pathophysiology: HSP is a Small-vessel vasculitis mediated by IgA immune complex deposition. IgA deposits weaken vessel walls, leading to purpura and bleeding. Because the platelet count is normal, also called as non-thrombocytopenic purpura . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
The clinical presentation of a 10-year-old child with palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, elevated serum IgA levels, and RBC casts in urine is suggestive of Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP).

  • Clinical features (PAAARpura):
    • P: Palpable purpura (typically lower extremities and buttocks)
    • A: Arthralgia / joint pain
    • A: Abdominal involvement (pain, nausea, GI bleeding possible)
    • A: Associated with elevated IgA (causative immunoglobulin)
    • R: Renal involvement (hematuria, red blood cell casts)
  • Pathophysiology: HSP is a Small-vessel vasculitis mediated by IgA immune complex deposition.
    • IgA deposits weaken vessel walls, leading to purpura and bleeding.
    • Because the platelet count is normal, also called as non-thrombocytopenic purpura.

An echocardiogram shows decreased left ventricular ejection fraction. Which of the following agents should be administered to prevent further cardiac damage?
questions.solution: The mechanism of cardiotoxicity by Daunorubicin is believed to be partly due to cardiac lipid peroxidation, which is promoted by Fe2+ causing Cardiomyopathy. Dexrazoxane is a cardioprotective, iron-chelating agent. It is used to prevent cardiotoxicity caused by the Anthracyclines like Daunorubicin and Doxorubicin. Dexrazoxane may also prevent anthracycline-derived DNA damage by interacting with topoisomerase II in cardiac cells. Penicillamine (Option A) is used for copper chelation and certain conditions like rheumatoid arthritis Dimercaprol (Option D) is used for arsenic and other heavy metal poisonings EDTA (Option C) is primarily used for lead poisoning. None of these agents provide the specific cardioprotective effects that dexrazoxane does against anthracycline-induced damage. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A patient is brought to the trauma unit after being assaulted. He presents with severe pain, swelling, and deformity in the lower jaw. Imaging confirms a "bucket handle" fracture of the mandible. What is the most likely nerve to be injured in this type of fracture?
questions.solution: lanation: Inferior alveolar nerve runs through the mandibular canal and is at risk of injury in fractures of the mandible, especially those involving the body of the mandible, like butterfly fractures. Butterfly Fractures of the Mandible: Also Known As : "Bucket handle" fractures. Type : Bilateral body fractures of the mandible. Common Causes : High-energy impacts (e.g., motor vehicle accidents, assaults). Main Complication : Airway obstruction. Characteristics and Mechanism: Appearance : Fracture creates a "butterfly" pattern. Impact : Significant compromise of mandible’s structural integrity. Injury Mechanism : Involves high-force trauma, potentially leading to additional injuries in surrounding tissues. Management Strategies: Method Indication Details Closed Reduction Non-displaced or minimally displaced fractures Uses intermaxillary fixation (MMF) for stabilization. Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF) Displaced fractures Surgical realignment and stabilization using plates/screws. Complications: Malocclusion : Misalignment of teeth. Non-union : Failure of the fracture to heal properly. Nerve Injury : Particularly to the inferior alveolar nerve, causing altered sensation in the lower lip. Lingual nerve (Option A) : This nerve is less likely to be injured in a mandibular body fracture as it is located more medially and higher up in the jaw. Hypoglossal nerve (Option C) : This nerve is involved in tongue movement and is not typically affected by mandible fractures. Facial nerve (Option D ) : The facial nerve controls facial muscles and is usually affected by fractures of the zygomatic arch or parotid area, not the mandible. @Neet_pg_bot

Method

Indication

Details

Closed Reduction

Non-displaced or minimally displaced fractures

Uses intermaxillary fixation (MMF) for stabilization.

Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF)

Displaced fractures

Surgical realignment and stabilization using plates/screws.

 

Complications:

  • Malocclusion: Misalignment of teeth.
  • Non-union: Failure of the fracture to heal properly.

The ADP-ATP translocase in the inner mitochondrial membrane exports ATP to the cytosol and imports ADP into the mitochondria.. Atractyloside inhibits this transport process. Function : It plays a crucial role in oxidative phosphorylation. Oxidation, which involves the loss of electrons, is central to this process and drives ATP synthesis Shuttles : NADH Shuttles: Glycolysis, which occurs in the cytoplasm, generates 2 NADH molecules per glucose molecule. NADH cannot directly cross the mitochondrial membrane; it requires shuttles for transport. There are two main shuttle systems: the malate-aspartate shuttle (Image 1) and the glycerol phosphate shuttle (Image 2), which facilitate NADH transport across the mitochondrial membrane Property Malate Shuttle (Option A ruled out) Glycerol Phosphate Shuttle Location Present in most cells except white muscle fibers and neurons. He is convinced that those he interacts with daily are not his real family, leading to significant anxiety and fear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: The scenario describes Capgras Syndrome , a type of delusional misidentificatio n where the individual irrationally believes that a familiar person, usually a close family member or spouse, has been replaced by an identical imposter . Intermetamorphosis (Option A) is characterised by delusions that individuals have swapped identities (psychological and physical transformation) while keeping the same appearance. Fregoli syndrome (Option C) is a delusional misidentification where the individual falsely believes that different people they encounter are actually the same person in disguise. Nihilistic syndrome (Option D) is a depressive delusion in which the patient denies the existence of their body, their mind, their loved ones and the world around them. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: z's method for age estimation from teeth simplified Gustafson's system and excluded two of the six criteria: root resorption and cementum apposition. Gustafson's Method: Developed by Gosta Gustafson, this method estimates age by evaluating six specific regressive changes in teeth: Attrition (A): Wear of the occlusal surface due to chewing, starting with enamel and progressing to dentin and pulp. Periodontosis (P): Retraction of the gums, exposing the root and neck of the tooth, leading to loosening. Secondary Dentin (S): Gradual deposition in the pulp cavity, reducing its size and potentially obliterating it. Cementum Apposition (C): Thickening of cementum around the root as the tooth shifts in position, with continuous deposition forming incremental lines. Root Resorption (R): Degradation of cementum and dentin at the root apex, progressing upwards. Root Transparency: Increased transparency in the root due to rarefaction of dentin, beginning from the apex and moving upward in lower teeth, and downward in upper teeth. This is considered the most reliable of all criteria. Each change is scored from 0 to 3, and the total score (Y) is used in the formula for age estimation . 0–No change 1–Beginning of change 2–Obvious change 3–Maximum change A + P + S + C + R + T = total score (Y) An increase in age shows a linear increase in the total score. The age is estimated using the following formula: Age = 11.43 + 4.56 × Y (total score) The method is most accurate for individuals between 25–60 years old. It requires extracting and microscopically examining a longitudinal section of the tooth, limiting its use to deceased individuals or skeletal remains. Dalitz's Method: Dalitz refined Gustafson’s method to improve accuracy by discarding less reliable factors like root resorption and secondary cementum apposition. He focused on scoring the following changes in the 12 anterior teeth on a 5-point scoring system from 0 to 4. Attrition (A) Periodontitis (P) Secondary Dentin Deposition (S) Root Transparency (T) While more accurate, the Dalitz method's main drawback is its limitation to anterior teeth, excluding bicuspid (premolars) and molars from analysis. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
z's method for age estimation from teeth simplified Gustafson's system and excluded two of the six criteria: root resorption and cementum apposition.

 

Gustafson's Method:

Developed by Gosta Gustafson, this method estimates age by evaluating six specific regressive changes in teeth:

  1. Attrition (A): Wear of the occlusal surface due to chewing, starting with enamel and progressing to dentin and pulp.
  2. Periodontosis (P): Retraction of the gums, exposing the root and neck of the tooth, leading to loosening.
  3. Secondary Dentin (S): Gradual deposition in the pulp cavity, reducing its size and potentially obliterating it.
  4. Cementum Apposition (C): Thickening of cementum around the root as the tooth shifts in position, with continuous deposition forming incremental lines.
  5. Root Resorption (R): Degradation of cementum and dentin at the root apex, progressing upwards.
  6. Root Transparency: Increased transparency in the root due to rarefaction of dentin, beginning from the apex and moving upward in lower teeth, and downward in upper teeth. This is considered the most reliable of all criteria.

 

Each change is scored from 0 to 3, and the total score (Y) is used in the formula for age estimation.

  • 0–No change
  • 1–Beginning of change
  • 2–Obvious change
  • 3–Maximum change

 

A + P + S + C + R + T = total score (Y)

 

An increase in age shows a linear increase in the total score. The age is estimated using the following formula:

 

Age = 11.43 + 4.56 × Y (total score)

 

  • The method is most accurate for individuals between 25–60 years old.
  • It requires extracting and microscopically examining a longitudinal section of the tooth, limiting its use to deceased individuals or skeletal remains.

 

Dalitz's Method:

Dalitz refined Gustafson’s method to improve accuracy by discarding less reliable factors like root resorption and secondary cementum apposition. He focused on scoring the following changes in the 12 anterior teeth on a 5-point scoring system from 0 to 4.

  1. Attrition (A)
  2. Periodontitis (P)
  3. Secondary Dentin Deposition (S)
  4. Root Transparency (T)

 

While more accurate, the Dalitz method's main drawback is its limitation to anterior teeth, excluding bicuspid (premolars) and molars from analysis.

questions.stem: A researcher is investigating the association between a new dietary supplement and the development of a rare type of cancer. The study includes 100 patients with the cancer and 100 healthy individuals. All of the following biases can occur in this type of study except?
questions.stemHtml: A researcher is investigating the association between a new dietary supplement and the development of a rare type of cancer. The study includes 100 patients with the cancer and 100 healthy individuals. All of the following biases can occur in this type of study except?
questions.solution: p> Explanation: Pygmalion Bias occurs when the researcher's expectations influence participant performance. This bias is irrelevant to case-control studies, which are retrospective and observational and more susceptible to biases like recall, selection, and ascertainment bias. Pygmalion Bias/ Rosenthal Effect: A phenomenon where higher researcher expectations increase participant performance or outcomes. Motivation is proportional to performance and gives an exaggerated response. Seen in experimental or educational settings. For example, increased motivation by teachers increases student performance. Recall Bias (Option A) occurs when participants do not accurately remember past events or experiences. It is common in case-control studies where cases might remember exposure more clearly than controls. Selection Bias (Option B) Happens when there is a systematic difference in characteristics between those selected for study and those not. It is possible that the cases and controls are not representative of the general population. Surveillance Bias or Ascertainment bias (Option C) Occurs when the disease or outcome is more likely to be identified in the exposed group because they are more closely monitored. This could occur if cases are more frequently monitored for dietary habits than controls. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
p>Explanation:

Pygmalion Bias occurs when the researcher's expectations influence participant performance. This bias is irrelevant to case-control studies, which are retrospective and observational and more susceptible to biases like recall, selection, and ascertainment bias.

 

Pygmalion Bias/ Rosenthal Effect:

  • A phenomenon where higher researcher expectations increase participant performance or outcomes.
  • Motivation is proportional to performance and gives an exaggerated response.
  • Seen in experimental or educational settings.
  • For example, increased motivation by teachers increases student performance.

 

Recall Bias (Option A) occurs when participants do not accurately remember past events or experiences.

  • It is common in case-control studies where cases might remember exposure more clearly than controls.

 

Selection Bias (Option B)

  • Happens when there is a systematic difference in characteristics between those selected for study and those not.
  • It is possible that the cases and controls are not representative of the general population.

 

Surveillance Bias or Ascertainment bias (Option C)

  • Occurs when the disease or outcome is more likely to be identified in the exposed group because they are more closely monitored.
  • This could occur if cases are more frequently monitored for dietary habits than controls.

What is the substrate concentration [S] of the given enzyme?
questions.solution: The substrate concentration [S] represents the amount of substrate available for the enzyme to act upon in a given reaction. It is typically measured in units of concentration, such as micromoles per liter (µM) or millimoles per liter (mM). To find the substrate concentration [S], you can use the Michaelis-Menten equation: Vo = Vmax[S] / Km + [S] Given: (Vmax): 100 µmol/min (Km): 10 µM (Vo): 50 µmol/min Substitute the given values into the equation: 50 = 100[S] / 10+ [S] 50 (10 + [S]) = 100 [S] Simplify and solve for [S]: 500 + 50[S] = 100[S] 500 = 50[S] [S] = 10 µM Therefore, the substrate concentration [S] is 10 µM. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
The substrate concentration [S] represents the amount of substrate available for the enzyme to act upon in a given reaction. It is typically measured in units of concentration, such as micromoles per liter (µM) or millimoles per liter (mM).

 

To find the substrate concentration [S], you can use the Michaelis-Menten equation:

 

Vo = Vmax[S]/Km + [S]

 

Given:

(Vmax): 100 µmol/min

(Km): 10 µM

(Vo): 50 µmol/min

 

Substitute the given values into the equation:

 

50 = 100[S]/10+ [S]

 

50 (10 + [S]) = 100 [S]

 

Simplify and solve for [S]:

 

500 + 50[S] = 100[S]

 

500 = 50[S]

 

[S] = 10 µM

 

Therefore, the substrate concentration [S] is 10 µM.

Systemic effects, uses and C/I of Ketamine

System

Effects

CNS
  • It is associated with increased cerebral oxygen consumption, blood flow, and intracranial pressure.
  • It causes functional disorganization by selectively depressing neuronal activity in the cortex and thalamus while stimulating the limbic system, leading to disrupted pain perception and emotional processing.
  • Emergence reactions, including vivid dreams, hallucinations, and illusion, occurs due to depression of auditory and visual relay nuclei,
  • It provides analgesia, amnesia, and unconsciousness, making it a "complete" anesthetic.

CVS
  • Increases arterial blood pressure, heart rate, and cardiac output, particularly after rapid bolus injections.
  • Stimulates the sympathetic nervous system and inhibits norepinephrine reuptake, increasing pulmonary artery pressure and myocardial workload.
  • Direct myocardial depression can occur with sympathetic blockade or catecholamine depletion.

Respiratory
  • Racemic ketamine is a strong bronchodilator, useful in asthmatic patients.
  • Upper airway reflexes remain intact.
  • Excessive salivation can be managed with anticholinergics (e.g., glycopyrrolate).

Muscle

Uses:

  • Induction & Maintenance: Effective for unstable cardiovascular patients (e.g., hypovolemia, trauma, sepsis).
  • Combines with propofol or midazolam to reduce side effects (tachycardia, hypertension) and stabilize hemodynamics.

  • IV induction agent of choice in bronchial asthma

  • Preventive Analgesia: Small doses (20-60 mg) reduce postoperative pain and opioid consumption.
  • Used for chronic pain (e.g., cancer pain, neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia)
  • Procedures & Emergency Use: Common in emergency departments and short painful procedures.

Contraindications:

  • Increased ICP (Head injury, neuro surgery) 
  • Epilepsy
  • Ischemic heart disease, vascular aneurysms
  • Open eye injuries, and
  • Schizophrenia.

questions.solution: customMeta" data-dictid="d7bb0026fe169277719321db7b41a2">neonate presenting with facial rashes exacerbated by sunlight exposure, along with a maternal history of positive anti-Ro/SSA antibodies, is highly suggestive of neonatal lupus erythematosus (NLE). Clinical features of Neonatal Lupus Erythematosus are: Cutaneous: Rash resembling subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) or discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE). Owl’s eye sign or Racoon sign- Erythematous, slightly scaly eruption on the face and periorbital skin Cardiac: Various degrees of heart block, including first-degree, second-degree, or complete heart block. A complete heart block may require pacemaker placement. Hepatic involvement: Hepatitis cholestasis, Hematological abnormalities: Thrombocytopenia Anemia Neurological manifestations: seizures Developmental delay. Respiratory manifestations: Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) Transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN), Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies, also known as anti-SSA and anti-SSB antibodies are commonly implicated in neonatal systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and also Sjögren's syndrome. Incorrect Answer Explanation Option B: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is commonly seen in premature infants and is associated with conditions such as respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), and bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). Option C: Coarctation of the aorta can occur in the context of Turner syndrome. Option D: Aortic stenosis occurs in Williams Syndrome (Chromosome 7 defect) @Neet_pg_bot

tomMeta" data-dictid="337d16dac5169277718474b97f6e4a">Circulation Following Birth:

 

Parameter/Structure

Change

Cause

Pulmonary Vascular Resistance (PVR)

Decreases

(Option A ruled out)

Mechanical expansion of the lungs and increased arterial PO2 lead to a rapid decrease in PVR.

Systemic Vascular Resistance (SVR)

Increases

The removal of the low-resistance placental circulation results in an increase in SVR.

Ductus Arteriosus Shunt

Reverses and eventually closes.
  • As PVR becomes lower than SVR, the shunt through the ductus arteriosus reverses from right-to-left to left-to-right.
  • High arterial PO2 leads to the constriction and eventual closure of the ductus arteriosus, which later becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.

Foramen Ovale

Closes

Increased pulmonary blood flow to the left atrium raises left atrial volume and pressure, leading to the functional closure of the foramen ovale.

Ductus Venosus

Closes

(Option C ruled out)

The removal of the placenta from circulation results in the closure of the ductus venosus.

Left ventricular Wall Thickness and Mass

Increases

(Option B ruled out)

The left ventricle's wall thickness and mass increase as it adapts to the high-resistance systemic circulation.

Right ventricular Wall Thickness and Mass

Decreases

(Option D)

The right ventricle's wall thickness and mass decrease as it adapts to the low-resistance pulmonary circulation.

Left Ventricular Output

Increases

The left ventricle now must deliver the entire systemic cardiac output, which is almost a 200% increase compared to fetal conditions.

Right Ventricular Output

Increases

Opening of pulmonary vasculature results in increased right ventricular output.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a rule for criminally insane individuals?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is NOT a rule for criminally insane individuals?
questions.solution: strong>Explanation: Morrison’s Rule is not a recognised rule related to the criminal responsibility of insane individuals. Morrison's Rule states that after five months of fetal development, the crown-heel length in centimetres can be divided by five to estimate the fetal age in months. This provides a simple method for assessing gestational age based on fetal size. Criminal responsibility of insane persons rules: Durham’s Rule (1954) : An accused is not criminally responsible if their unlawful act results from a mental disease or defect. (Option B ruled out) Curren’s Rule (1964) : An accused is not criminally responsible if, due to a mental disease or defect, they were unable to regulate their conduct according to the law at the time of the act. (Option A ruled out) American Law Institute Test (1970) : A person is not responsible for criminal actions if, due to mental disease or defect, they lack adequate capacity to understand the wrongfulness of their actions or to conform to legal requirements. (Option C ruled out) Brawner Rule (1972) : Insanity determinations should be made by a jury, which has the discretion to decide the "insanity question." The Irresistible Impulse : This rule posits that an individual may recognize an act as illegal but, due to mental impairment, cannot control their actions. For example, Lorena Bobbitt was acquitted in 1994 by arguing that an irresistible impulse led her to commit her crime. @Neet_pg_bot

Morrison’s Rule is not a recognised rule related to the criminal responsibility of insane individuals.

Morrison's Rule states that after five months of fetal development, the crown-heel length in centimetres can be divided by five to estimate the fetal age in months. This provides a simple method for assessing gestational age based on fetal size.

 

Criminal responsibility of insane persons rules:

 

  • Durham’s Rule (1954): An accused is not criminally responsible if their unlawful act results from a mental disease or defect. (Option B ruled out)
  • Curren’s Rule (1964): An accused is not criminally responsible if, due to a mental disease or defect, they were unable to regulate their conduct according to the law at the time of the act. (Option A ruled out)
  • American Law Institute Test (1970): A person is not responsible for criminal actions if, due to mental disease or defect, they lack adequate capacity to understand the wrongfulness of their actions or to conform to legal requirements. (Option C ruled out)
  • Brawner Rule (1972): Insanity determinations should be made by a jury, which has the discretion to decide the "insanity question."
  • The Irresistible Impulse: This rule posits that an individual may recognize an act as illegal but, due to mental impairment, cannot control their actions. For example, Lorena Bobbitt was acquitted in 1994 by arguing that an irresistible impulse led her to commit her crime.

rat-Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PMJAY), a scheme of the Government of India designed to provide health insurance coverage to economically disadvantaged families.

 

Ayushman Bharat - Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PMJAY):

  • An initiative launched in 2018 by Govt. of India to achieve UHC
  • Provides all the elements, including NCDS, in primary care.

The National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) (Option D) provides accessible, affordable, and quality healthcare to the rural population, reducing mortality rates and disease transmission.

questions.solution: 3583">cross-linking (CXL) Explanation: The patient has keratoconus showing progressive ectasia. Corneal collagen cross-linking (CXL) with riboflavin is the most appropriate treatment for stabilizing keratoconus progression and improving contact lens tolerance in this patient. It works by strengthening the corneal stroma through the cross-linking of collagen fibers, which helps to halt the progression of ectasia, thereby preserving vision and enhancing the effectiveness of contact lenses. Treatment of Keratoconus Spectacle Correction (Option A) : Effective in the early stages, but contact lenses are more beneficial. Less effective in later stages due to irregular astigmatism. Treatment of Keratoconus

questions.stem: Histopathological examination of a lesion arising from the right distal femur is given as the image below with such characteristic cells. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: Histopathological examination of a lesion arising from the right distal femur is given as the image below with such characteristic cells. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.solution: on: The histopathological image shows numerous multinucleated giant cells , along with mononuclear cells scattered in the background in a bone lesion, suggesting osteoclastoma/giant cell tumour. Giant cell tumour (Osteoclastoma): It is a benign but locally aggressive tumour characterised by numerous multinucleated osteoclast-type giant cells. The neoplastic component is made up of the mononuclear cells , while the multinucleated giant cells are only a reactionary or secondary component . Giant cell tumours develop within the epiphysis and may extend into the metaphysis. Mostly located near the knee, involving the distal femur or proximal tibia. Although rare, they can metastasize to the lungs , but typically regress spontaneously and are rarely fatal. Morphology: Grossly, the tumours are large , red-brown masses that frequently undergo cystic degeneration. Chondrosarcoma (Option B): S hows malignant cartilage, which is recognised by the presence of multiple cartilage cells within a single lacuna, Osteochondroma (Option C): It classically shows both bone (osteo) and cartilage components together. Ewing’s sarcoma (Option D): This belongs to the group of small round blue cell tumors . On histology, we would see sheets of small blue cells and the characteristic Homer Wright pseudorosettes , none of which are seen here. @Neet_pg_bot

Giant cell tumour (Osteoclastoma):

  • The neoplastic component is made up of the mononuclear cells, while the multinucleated giant cells are only a reactionary or secondary component.
  • Giant cell tumours develop within the epiphysis and may extend into the metaphysis.
    • Mostly located near the knee, involving the distal femur or proximal tibia.
    • Although rare, they can metastasize to the lungs, but typically regress spontaneously and are rarely fatal.
  • Morphology:
    • Grossly, the tumours are large, red-brown masses that frequently undergo cystic degeneration.

Chondrosarcoma (Option B): Shows malignant cartilage, which is recognised by the presence of multiple cartilage cells within a single lacuna,

Osteochondroma (Option C): It classically shows both bone (osteo) and cartilage components together.

Ewing’s sarcoma (Option D): This belongs to the group of small round blue cell tumors. On histology, we would see sheets of small blue cells and the characteristic Homer Wright pseudorosettes, none of which are seen here.

The Lautenschlaeger technique specifically involves medial displacement of the lateral nasal wall to narrow the nasal cavities, which can help reduce crusting by improving airflow and humidifying the nasal passages in patients with atrophic rhinitis. Treatment of Atrophic Rhinitis: Treatment focuses on symptom management, especially foul smell and crusting, and aims to improve quality of life. Both medical and surgical approaches are used. Medical Treatment: Treatment Details Nasal Irrigation and Crust Removal Use warm normal saline or an alkaline solution for nasal irrigation. Irrigate multiple times daily initially, reducing to once every 2-3 days as symptoms improve. For stubborn crusts, use glucose-glycerin solution before removal with forceps or suction. Antibiotics Systemic antibiotics (e.g., fluoroquinolones with metronidazole) for 7-10 days. Long-term use is not recommended. Other Therapies Mucolytics: Potassium iodide solutions to liquefy secretions. Experimental: Oestradiol nasal sprays and submucosal placental extract injections have been explored. Surgical Treatment: Procedure Details Young's Operation and Modifications Complete closure of both nostrils in the nasal vestibule. Reopen nostrils after approximately 6 months to encourage mucosal regeneration and reduce crusting. Modified versions partially close nostrils to reduce discomfort while aiming for similar benefits. ss="customMeta" data-dictid="31c5d0e75f16927771938d8e2daa4c">nasal crusting and a foul odour due to the atrophy of the nasal mucosa.

 

The Lautenschlaeger technique specifically involves medial displacement of the lateral nasal wall to narrow the nasal cavities, which can help reduce crusting by improving airflow and humidifying the nasal passages in patients with atrophic rhinitis.

 

Treatment of Atrophic Rhinitis:

Treatment focuses on symptom management, especially foul smell and crusting, and aims to improve quality of life. Both medical and surgical approaches are used.

Medical Treatment:

Treatment

Details

Nasal Irrigation and Crust Removal
  • Use warm normal saline or an alkaline solution for nasal irrigation.
  • Irrigate multiple times daily initially, reducing to once every 2-3 days as symptoms improve.
  • For stubborn crusts, use glucose-glycerin solution before removal with forceps or suction.

Topical Applications

Apply 25% glucose in glycerine to inhibit proteolytic bacteria growth, reducing foul smell.

Antibiotics
  • Systemic antibiotics (e.g., fluoroquinolones with metronidazole) for 7-10 days.
  • Long-term use is not recommended.

Other Therapies
  • Mucolytics: Potassium iodide solutions to liquefy secretions.
  • Experimental: Oestradiol nasal sprays and submucosal placental extract injections have been explored.

Dietary Recommendations

A balanced diet rich in vitamins A, D, folic acid, iron, and protein to support overall health and mucosal recovery.

 

Surgical Treatment:

 

Procedure

Details

Young's Operation and Modifications
  • Complete closure of both nostrils in the nasal vestibule.
  • Reopen nostrils after approximately 6 months to encourage mucosal regeneration and reduce crusting.
  • Modified versions partially close nostrils to reduce discomfort while aiming for similar benefits.

Techniques to narrow excessively wide nasal chambers
  • Autologous grafts (fat, cartilage, bone) placed under the mucoperiosteum of nasal floor/lateral walls or mucoperichondrium of septum.
  • Allografts (Alloderm, Cymetra) can be used.
  • The Lautenschlaeger technique involves medial displacement of the lateral nasal wall to narrow nasal cavities which can help reduce crusting by improving airflow and humidifying the nasal passages. (Option D)

 

Young's operation and its modifications (Option A): Involves closing and then reopening the nostrils to promote mucosal regeneration and reduce crusting, not specifically for narrowing nasal cavities.

Use of 25% glucose in glycerine nasal application (Option B): Helps inhibit bacterial growth and reduce odour, not related to narrowing nasal cavities.

Nasal irrigation with an alkaline solution (Option C): Aimed at crust removal and odour reduction, not for narrowing nasal cavities.

questions.stemHtml: A 35 year old woman presents with severe breathlessness, palpitations, and swelling in her legs and face. She primarily eats white rice and lacks fruits and vegetables in her diet. On examination and investigations she has distended neck veins, peripheral edema, and elevated lactate and pyruvate levels. questions.solution: Thiamine Deficiency Aleurone layer of cereals (food grains) is a rich source of thiamine. Whole wheat flour and unpolished hand-pound rice have better nutritive value than completely polished refined foods. Polishing grains removes the aleurone layer, reducing thiamine content. Deficiency Manifestations Dry Beriberi More common CNS manifestations Pain, paresthesia, and loss of reflexes Peripheral neuritis with sensory disturbances (Option A ruled out) Wet Beriberi Cardiovascular symptoms : breathlessness, palpitations, and peripheral edema Distended neck veins observed High-output cardiac failure due to vasodilation (Option C) Biochemical Parameters Thiamine deficiency affects transketolase , an enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway . Measuring erythrocyte transketolase activity is a specific diagnostic test for thiamine deficiency (Option C). Earliest biochemical change : Reduced erythrocyte transketolase activity, even before clinical symptoms appear. Recommended Daily Allowance : 1–1.5 mg/day Condition-Wise Role of Thiamine and Deficiency Effects Condition Biochemical Role of Thiamine Deficiency Manifestations Dry Beriberi (Option A ruled out) Essential for carbohydrate metabolism and nerve function Peripheral neuritis, sensory disturbances, difficulty walking, paralysis due to CNS involvement. Wet Beriberi Thiamine is required for pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex ; deficiency leads to lactic acidosis , causing vasodilation and cardiovascular symptoms Edema, palpitations, breathlessness, heart failure Maple Syrup Urine Disease (Option B ruled out) Cofactor for decarboxylation of branched-chain keto acids Accumulation of branched-chain keto acids , causing convulsions, mental retardation, vomiting, acidosis, coma, and death Lactic Acidosis (Option D ruled out) Cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase , which converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA Impaired pyruvate metabolism , leading to increased lactate and pyruvate , causing lactic acidosis @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Thiamine Deficiency

  • Aleurone layer of cereals (food grains) is a rich source of thiamine. Whole wheat flour and unpolished hand-pound rice have better nutritive value than completely polished refined foods.
  • Polishing grains removes the aleurone layer, reducing thiamine content.

Deficiency Manifestations

Dry Beriberi

  • More common CNS manifestations
  • Pain, paresthesia, and loss of reflexes
  • Peripheral neuritis with sensory disturbances (Option A ruled out)

Wet Beriberi

  • Cardiovascular symptoms: breathlessness, palpitations, and peripheral edema
  • Distended neck veins observed
  • High-output cardiac failure due to vasodilation (Option C)

Biochemical Parameters

  • Thiamine deficiency affects transketolase, an enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway.
  • Measuring erythrocyte transketolase activity is a specific diagnostic test for thiamine deficiency (Option C).
  • Earliest biochemical change: Reduced erythrocyte transketolase activity, even before clinical symptoms appear.
  • Recommended Daily Allowance: 1–1.5 mg/day

Condition-Wise Role of Thiamine and Deficiency Effects

Condition Biochemical Role of Thiamine Deficiency Manifestations
Dry Beriberi (Option A ruled out) Essential for carbohydrate metabolism and nerve function Peripheral neuritis, sensory disturbances, difficulty walking, paralysis due to CNS involvement.
Wet Beriberi Thiamine is required for pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex; deficiency leads to lactic acidosis, causing vasodilation and cardiovascular symptoms Edema, palpitations, breathlessness, heart failure
Maple Syrup Urine Disease (Option B ruled out) Cofactor for decarboxylation of branched-chain keto acids Accumulation of branched-chain keto acids, causing convulsions, mental retardation, vomiting, acidosis, coma, and death
Lactic Acidosis (Option D ruled out) Cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, which converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA Impaired pyruvate metabolism, leading to increased lactate and pyruvate, causing lactic acidosis

exual intercourse by a man with his wife if she is not under 18 years of age (old definition not under 15 years) is not considered as rape.

Rape:

BNS

BNS 63 (Old: Section 375 IPC)

Definition

Unlawful sexual intercourse by a man with a woman through force or under certain conditions

Acts considered

  • Penetrates his penis into the vagina, mouth, urethra, or anus
  • Inserts any object or body part (not his penis) or applies his mouth to the vagina, mouth, urethra, or anus (Option A ruled out) (Option D ruled out)
  • Manipulates any part of the woman's body to cause penetration into the vagina, urethra, or anus (Option B ruled out)

Circumstances

  • Against her will
  • Without her consent
  • With her consent obtained through fear of death or hurt
  • With her consent, when she believes he is her husband due to impersonation
  • When she cannot understand the nature of consent due to unsoundness of mind, intoxication, or being drugged
  • Statutory rape: With or without her consent, if she is under 18 years of age
  • When she is unable to communicate consent

Exception

  • Medical interventions or procedures
  • Sexual intercourse by a man with his wife if she is not under 18 years of age (Option C)

questions.solution: tid="d398f22bb71692777201622867bda7">Triangle is designed to help identify and preserve the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN) during surgery. Joll’s Triangle (Sternothyroid-laryngeal triangle) An anatomical landmark used for identifying and preserving the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN). Superior border by the upper attachment of the strap muscles. Medial border by the midline of the neck. Lateral border by the upper pole of the thyroid gland and the superior thyroid vessels. Floor of the Triangle: The EBSLN is located in the floor of the triangle, which is delineated by the cricothyroid muscle. questions.solutionHtml:
tid="d398f22bb71692777201622867bda7">Triangle is designed to help identify and preserve the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN) during surgery.

 

Joll’s Triangle (Sternothyroid-laryngeal triangle)

An anatomical landmark used for identifying and preserving the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN).

  • Superior border by the upper attachment of the strap muscles.
  • Medial border by the midline of the neck.
  • Lateral border by the upper pole of the thyroid gland and the superior thyroid vessels.
  • Floor of the Triangle: The EBSLN is located in the floor of the triangle, which is delineated by the cricothyroid muscle.


 

Joll’s Triangle is not used for locating the Recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option A) or Internal Branch of the Superior Laryngeal Nerve (Option C) or Vagus Nerve (Option D).

strong>Gestational diabetes that is well-controlled with diet and exercise alone is not an indication for a C-section. Women with GDM can often have a vaginal delivery if there are no other complications. If controlled, there is no significant risk to the mother or fetus.

questions.solutionHtml:
is diagnosed as Weber's Syndrome, which is characterized by right-sided hemiparesis, ight-sided paralysis of the lower face, left-sided ptosis and a "down and out" position of the left eye.
  • This syndrome impacts the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III) nucleus and corticospinal fibers, leading to the loss of the medial lemniscus, red nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle, and oculomotor nerve fibers.
  • Characteristic features:
    • Ipsilateral squint (pupil points downwards and laterally) due to injury to the oculomotor nerve.
    • Contralateral hemiplegia due to involvement of corticospinal tract.
    • Involvement of the rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (riMLF) in the midbrain causes Weber syndrome with vertical gaze palsy.

    • Horner’s syndrome (Option A) is caused by damage to the cervical sympathetic trunk, which is characterized by:

    • Ptosis (drooping of the upper eyelid)
    • Miosis (constriction of the pupil)
    • Anhydrosis (loss of sweating on that side of the face)
    • Enophthalmos (retraction of the eyeball)
    • Loss of the ciliospinal reflex (pinching the skin on the nape of the neck does not cause pupil dilation, which typically occurs).


     

    Benedikt’s syndrome (Option B) is due to damage to most of the tegmentum of the midbrain, which is characterized by:

    • Loss of proprioception due to the lesion of the medial lemniscus
    • The pupil points downwards and laterally due to injury to the third nerve
    • Tremors and twitching of opposite side due to damage to the red nucleus and superior cerebellar peduncle.



     

    Parinaud’s syndrome (Option C) is due to a lesion of the superior colliculi (as shown in the above image), characterised by weakness of upward gaze and vertical nystagmus due to involvement of the superior colliculus.
